er-s026.x: Sunlight looks white, but it is a mixture of all the colours of the rainbow, each with a different wavelength. Violet and blue light have the shortest wavelengths; red has the longest. When sunlight enters the atmosphere, it meets countless molecules of nitrogen and oxygen, which are far smaller than the wavelength of visible light. Such tiny particles scatter light in all directions, but they do not treat every colour equally: shorter wavelengths are scattered much more strongly than longer ones. This effect is called Rayleigh scattering, after the British physicist Lord Rayleigh, who worked out its mathematics in the nineteenth century. Because blue light is scattered so strongly, it reaches our eyes from every part of the sky, and the whole sky appears blue. Violet is scattered even more, so why is the sky not violet? Part of the answer is that sunlight contains less violet than blue, some violet is absorbed high in the atmosphere, and our eyes are less sensitive to violet. At sunrise and sunset, sunlight travels a much longer path through the air to reach us. Along the way most of the blue is scattered out of the direct beam, so the light that remains is rich in orange and red. Larger particles, such as the water droplets in clouds, scatter all colours about equally, which is why clouds look white or grey rather than blue.

er-s027.x: For most of history, units of measurement varied from place to place. A foot or a pound in one town might differ from the foot or pound in the next, and traders, builders and scientists constantly had to convert between local standards. In the 1790s, scientists in France set out to design a system that would be the same for everyone and based on nature rather than on custom. They defined the metre as one ten-millionth of the distance from the North Pole to the equator, measured along a line passing through Paris, and two surveyors spent several years measuring part of that distance. Units of volume and mass were linked to the metre: a litre was the volume of a cube one-tenth of a metre on each side, and a kilogram was close to the mass of a litre of water. Above all, larger and smaller units were related by powers of ten, so converting kilometres to metres needed only a shift of the decimal point. The new system was slow to win acceptance, even in France, because people were attached to familiar units. Over the following two centuries, however, it spread across the world and became the basis of the International System of Units used in science today. Its definitions have since been refined: the metre is now fixed by the speed of light, which can be measured far more precisely than the size of the Earth.

er-s028.x: Most substances shrink as they cool and are densest in their solid form, so a solid piece usually sinks in its own liquid. Water is a striking exception. As water cools, it becomes denser only until it reaches about 4 °C; below that temperature it begins to expand again, and when it freezes it expands by roughly nine per cent. Ice is therefore less dense than liquid water, and it floats. The explanation lies in hydrogen bonding. In liquid water, molecules are constantly forming and breaking weak bonds with their neighbours, which lets them pack fairly closely. In ice, each molecule is held by hydrogen bonds to four others in a fixed, open pattern that contains a great deal of empty space. This odd behaviour has large consequences. In winter, the surface of a lake cools first. Water at 4 °C sinks to the bottom, and the colder water stays on top, where it eventually freezes. The layer of ice then acts like a lid, insulating the water below, so that lakes in cold regions freeze from the top down and seldom freeze solid. Fish and other creatures can survive the winter in the liquid water beneath. The same expansion causes trouble for people: water that freezes inside a pipe or a crack in a rock can split it open, which is why water pipes in cold places are buried or wrapped.

er-s029.x: Deosai, in Gilgit-Baltistan, is one of the highest plateaus in the world, a rolling plain that lies at an average height of roughly 4,000 metres above sea level. For more than half the year it is buried under deep snow and almost no one goes there. When the snow melts in early summer, the plateau changes completely: streams fill with clear meltwater, and the grassland is covered with wild flowers that bloom quickly during the short growing season. The plateau was declared a national park in 1993, largely to protect the Himalayan brown bear, whose numbers had fallen very low because of hunting and disturbance. Brown bears spend the long winter in dens, living on fat stored during summer, when they feed on grasses, roots and small mammals such as marmots. Golden marmots are themselves among the most noticeable animals on Deosai, whistling a warning from the entrances of their burrows when a person or predator approaches. Since the park was created, regular monitoring has recorded a gradual rise in bear numbers. The plateau's growing popularity with summer visitors brings its own pressures, however. Jeeps that leave the tracks can damage the thin soil, which recovers only slowly in such a cold climate, and litter left near the lakes may draw bears towards people. Careful management of tourism is therefore now seen as part of protecting the park.

er-s030.x: When money is saved or invested at compound interest, the interest earned each year is added to the total, and the following year's interest is calculated on that larger amount. Growth of this kind speeds up over time, and it can be hard to judge in one's head how quickly a sum will grow. Bankers and economists therefore use a simple shortcut known as the rule of 72. To estimate how many years it takes for an amount to double, divide 72 by the yearly percentage rate of growth. At 6 per cent a year, savings double in about 12 years; at 9 per cent, in about 8 years. The rule is only an approximation, but for rates between about 2 and 15 per cent it is usually accurate to within a year. The number 72 is chosen partly because it divides neatly by many small whole numbers, such as 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 9 and 12, which makes mental arithmetic easy. The same shortcut works for anything that grows at a steady percentage rate. If a town's population rises by 3 per cent a year, it will double in about 24 years. It also works for prices: if prices rise by 8 per cent a year, money loses half its buying power in roughly 9 years. The rule cannot predict what future rates will be, but it turns an abstract percentage into a period of time that people can picture.

er-s031.x: A refrigerator does not create cold. It works by moving heat out of its insides and releasing it into the kitchen, and it does this with a fluid called a refrigerant that is pumped round a closed loop of pipes. The key to the process is that a liquid absorbs heat when it evaporates, which is why wet skin feels cool in a breeze. Inside the fridge, the refrigerant flows through coils as a cold liquid at low pressure. It boils easily, and as it turns into vapour it takes heat from the food and the air around it. The vapour then passes to a compressor, a pump driven by an electric motor, which squeezes it into a smaller volume. Compression makes the vapour hot, hotter than the room, so when it flows through the coils at the back or bottom of the fridge, it gives up its heat to the kitchen air and condenses into a liquid again. Finally, the liquid passes through a narrow opening into a region of low pressure, where it cools sharply and is ready to begin the cycle once more. Because the heat removed from the food ends up in the room, together with the heat produced by the motor, leaving the fridge door open on a hot day actually makes a kitchen warmer, not cooler. For the same reason, a fridge works best with space around its back coils, so that the heat can escape.

er-s032.x: For more than a thousand years, no one could read the hieroglyphs carved on the temples and tombs of ancient Egypt. The knowledge had been lost, and many scholars believed the signs were purely symbolic pictures that stood for ideas rather than sounds. The breakthrough came from a slab of dark stone found in 1799 near the town of Rashid, known in English as Rosetta, in the Nile Delta. The stone carried the same official decree written three times: in hieroglyphs, in Demotic, a later everyday Egyptian script, and in ancient Greek, which scholars could still read. The Greek text acted as a key. The English scientist Thomas Young made early progress, showing that some signs enclosed in oval rings, called cartouches, spelled the names of rulers such as Ptolemy. The French scholar Jean-François Champollion went much further. He knew Coptic, a late form of the Egyptian language, and used it to work out the sounds of many signs. In 1822 he announced that hieroglyphic writing mixed signs that stand for sounds with signs that stand for whole words or ideas, which is why earlier attempts that treated every sign as a picture had failed. His work opened thousands of inscriptions to study, and with them much of the history of ancient Egypt. The Rosetta Stone itself is now kept in the British Museum in London.

er-s033.x: The octopus is a mollusc, a relative of snails and clams, yet it behaves in ways that seem surprisingly clever. In aquariums, octopuses have learned to unscrew the lids of jars to reach food inside, and some have escaped from their tanks by squeezing through tiny gaps, since their bodies contain no bones and their only hard part is a beak. In the wild, certain species collect halves of coconut shells and carry them about to use as shelters. Their nervous system is organised very differently from ours. An octopus has roughly 500 million nerve cells, but about two-thirds of them are located in its eight arms rather than in its central brain. Each arm can therefore touch, taste and respond to its surroundings with a degree of independence, so the brain does not need to direct every movement. The animal is also a master of disguise. Special cells in its skin allow it to change colour and pattern in a fraction of a second, matching rocks, sand or seaweed, and some species can even change the texture of their skin. Other unusual features include three hearts and blue blood, which carries oxygen using a copper-based compound instead of the iron-based haemoglobin found in human blood. Despite all this ability, most octopuses live only one or two years, so whatever they know must be learned quickly and largely without help from parents.

er-s034.x: Lightning and thunder are produced by the same event, yet we usually see the flash before we hear the rumble. The reason is the great difference in the speeds of light and sound. Light travels so fast that the flash reaches an observer almost instantly, while sound in air covers only about 340 metres each second. Counting the seconds between flash and thunder therefore gives a rough measure of distance: a gap of three seconds means the lightning struck about one kilometre away. Thunder itself is the sound of air being heated suddenly. A lightning channel is only a few centimetres wide, but within a tiny fraction of a second it heats the air to tens of thousands of degrees, several times hotter than the surface of the Sun. The air expands so violently that it sends out a shock wave, which we hear as a sharp crack nearby or as a long rumble farther away. The rumbling happens because a lightning channel is several kilometres long, so sound from different parts of it arrives at slightly different times and also echoes off hills and buildings. Safety advice follows from these facts. If thunder can be heard, the storm is close enough for lightning to reach you, because strikes can occur many kilometres from the centre of a storm. People are therefore advised to go indoors when they first hear thunder and to stay there until it has stopped for some time.

er-s035.t: The pull of the first number
er-s035.x: Imagine two groups of shoppers asked to guess the price of a second-hand bicycle. Before guessing, the first group is asked whether the bicycle is worth more or less than 30,000 rupees; the second group is asked the same question with a figure of 8,000 rupees. In experiments of this kind, the first group usually gives much higher estimates than the second, even though both groups see the same bicycle and know that the opening figure is merely a starting point. Psychologists call this tendency anchoring: an initial number, once heard, pulls later judgements towards itself. The effect was described in the 1970s by the psychologists Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman, who found that even a number produced by spinning a wheel could influence people's estimates of unrelated quantities. Anchoring appears in many everyday settings. A shopkeeper who first shows a very expensive model makes the next one seem reasonable; a seller who opens a negotiation with a high price often ends with a higher agreed price than one who opens low. Experts are not immune, although knowledge of a subject can reduce the effect. One way to resist anchoring is to form your own estimate before hearing anyone else's figure; another is to consider deliberately why the anchor might be wrong. Neither method removes the influence entirely, but both make it weaker.

er-s036.x: The dromedary, or one-humped camel, is found across the dry lands of North Africa, the Middle East and South Asia, including the Thar and Cholistan deserts of Pakistan. A common belief is that its hump is a store of water. In fact, the hump is mostly fat. Keeping fat in one place, rather than spread under the skin, lets heat escape more easily from the rest of the body, and the fat can be broken down for energy when food is scarce. The camel's real skill with water lies elsewhere. Its kidneys produce very concentrated urine, and its dung is so dry that it contains little water. Moisture in its breath is partly recaptured inside its nose rather than lost to the air. A camel can also allow its body temperature to rise by several degrees during the day and fall again at night, so it does not need to sweat until it is very hot. Together these features let it survive the loss of a quarter or more of its body's water, an amount that would kill most mammals. Its red blood cells are oval rather than round, which helps them keep flowing when the blood thickens and resist bursting when the animal finally drinks. And drink it does: a thirsty camel can take in more than 100 litres of water in a few minutes.

er-s037.x: In 1994, an engineer named Masahiro Hara at Denso Wave, part of a Japanese group that made car components, faced a practical problem. Workers tracked parts using ordinary barcodes, which store information only in a single row of lines, so several barcodes often had to be scanned for one item. Hara's team designed a square code that stores data both across and down, which allows it to hold far more information in the same space. They called it the QR code, short for ‘quick response’. Three large squares sit in three of its corners. Wherever the code is placed, these squares tell a scanner which way up it is, so it can be read from any angle and at high speed. The pattern also contains extra, repeated information, so that a code which is partly dirty or torn can often still be read correctly. Denso Wave held a patent on the design but chose not to charge others for using it, a decision that helped the code spread far beyond car factories. The real turning point came when mobile phones gained cameras able to read codes directly. Today QR codes appear on restaurant menus, product labels, tickets and shop counters, where customers scan them to pay. Their convenience has one drawback: a code reveals nothing to the eye, so a fake sticker placed over a real one can send an unwary user to a harmful website.

er-s038.x: Cutting an onion is one of the few kitchen tasks that regularly brings people to tears, and the cause is a chemical defence. An intact onion contains sulfur compounds and an enzyme that acts on them, but the two are kept apart in different parts of its cells. When a knife breaks the cells open, they mix. A rapid series of reactions follows, and within about thirty seconds the onion releases a gas with the long name syn-propanethial-S-oxide. The gas drifts upwards and reaches the eyes, where it stimulates nerves in the surface of the eye. The brain responds by producing tears to wash the irritant away. For the plant, this system is useful: an animal that bites into an onion bulb receives an unpleasant surprise and may well leave the rest alone. For cooks, a few simple measures help. Chilling an onion before cutting slows the reactions and makes the gas less volatile. A very sharp knife crushes fewer cells than a blunt one, so less of the enzyme and sulfur compounds meet. Working beside an open window or under a kitchen fan carries the gas away from the face. Cooking, finally, destroys the enzyme, which is why fried or boiled onions never sting the eyes. Plant breeders have also developed onion varieties that produce much less of the gas.

er-s039.x: For most of history, mechanical clocks were poor timekeepers, often gaining or losing a quarter of an hour in a single day. The change came from a simple observation. In the late sixteenth century, the Italian scientist Galileo Galilei noticed that a pendulum takes almost the same time for each swing whether it swings widely or only a little, as long as the swings are small. Later work showed that the time of a swing depends on the pendulum's length, not on the weight of the bob at its end. A longer pendulum swings more slowly: to double the time of each swing, the length must be made four times as great. Galileo did not build a working pendulum clock, but in 1656 the Dutch scientist Christiaan Huygens did. His clocks used the steady swing of a pendulum to control the rate at which the gears turned, and the best of them were accurate to within about fifteen seconds a day. Further improvements followed. One stubborn problem was temperature: a metal rod expands slightly in warm weather and contracts in cold. Clockmakers solved it with pendulums built from two different metals arranged so that their changes in length cancelled out. For almost three hundred years afterwards, until quartz and atomic clocks appeared in the twentieth century, the pendulum clock remained the most accurate way of keeping time.

er-s040.x: Some of the driest places on Earth are not short of water in the air. Along parts of the coast of Chile and Peru, and in the mountains of southern Morocco, thick fog rolls in from the ocean on many days of the year, yet almost no rain falls. Fog harvesting aims to capture this moisture. The method is simple: a large net of fine plastic mesh, stretched between two poles, is set up facing the wind on a hillside. As fog drifts through, tiny droplets strike the threads and stick to them. Many droplets merge into larger drops, which become heavy enough to run down the mesh into a gutter at the bottom and then through a pipe to a storage tank. A single square metre of net may collect a few litres on a good day, so villages use many nets together. The idea was partly inspired by a beetle of the Namib Desert that collects fog droplets on its back and lets them roll towards its mouth. Fog nets need no fuel or electricity and are cheap to maintain, but they work only where fog is frequent and the wind blows steadily in the right direction. They are therefore not a general answer to water shortage; rather, they are a useful source for particular communities that live in the right places.

er-s001.x: Along the coast south of Karachi, where the Indus finally meets the Arabian Sea, lies one of the largest arid-climate mangrove forests in the world. Mangroves are trees that tolerate salt water, and in the Indus delta a single species, Avicennia marina, makes up most of the forest. Its roots send small breathing tubes up through the mud, allowing the tree to take in air even when the soil is waterlogged and poor in oxygen. The forest matters far beyond its own boundaries. Its tangled roots slow incoming waves and hold sediment in place, so villages behind a healthy belt of mangroves suffer less damage when storms strike. The sheltered channels between the trees serve as nurseries where young fish and shrimp grow before moving to open water, which makes the forest important to the coastal fishing economy. Mangrove soils also lock away large amounts of carbon, often more per hectare than many inland forests. Yet mangroves depend on a delicate balance. They need fresh water and silt from the river as well as salt water from the sea. When less river water reaches the delta, the water becomes saltier and fewer seedlings survive. For this reason, people who replant mangroves along the Sindh coast pay close attention to whether some fresh water still reaches the mudflats they plant.

er-s002.x: In the dry valleys of Balochistan, farmers have for centuries drawn water from the ground without pumps or engines. Their method, the karez, is a gently sloping tunnel dug into the base of a hillside until it reaches water-bearing gravel. From there the tunnel carries groundwater, by gravity alone, to fields and villages that may lie several kilometres away. A line of vertical shafts, visible on the surface like a row of craters, marks its route; the shafts were used to remove soil during digging and still allow workers to climb down for cleaning. Because the water travels underground, very little of it is lost to evaporation, a great advantage in a region of hot summers and scarce rain. A karez also has a built-in limit: it can deliver only as much water as seeps into it, so it rarely drains an aquifer faster than rain and snowmelt refill it. Maintenance is shared, and families traditionally receive water in turns measured by time. In recent decades, many karezes have dried up. Electric and diesel tube wells, which can pump water from far deeper levels, have lowered the water table in several valleys. As the water table sinks below the tunnels, the old channels simply stop flowing, and the knowledge needed to maintain them begins to fade along with them.

er-s003.t: How vaccines use the body's memory
er-s003.x: When a virus or bacterium enters the body for the first time, the immune system needs several days to respond fully. Special white blood cells must recognise the invader, multiply and produce antibodies, proteins that attach to the germ and mark it for destruction. During this delay the person may become seriously ill. Once the infection is defeated, however, some of these cells remain in the body as memory cells. If the same germ returns, the memory cells recognise it at once, and the response is so fast and strong that the person often notices nothing at all. A vaccine makes use of this memory without the danger of the disease. It presents the immune system with a harmless version of the germ, or just one of its parts, such as a surface protein. Some vaccines contain killed germs, some contain weakened ones, and newer types give the body's cells instructions to make the protein themselves. In every case the immune system responds as if a real infection were under way and keeps memory cells afterwards. Vaccination also protects people who cannot be vaccinated, such as newborn babies or those with weakened immunity. When most of a community is immune, a germ finds too few hosts to spread, and outbreaks fade before they can reach the most vulnerable.

er-s004.x: Before the middle of the fifteenth century, every book in Europe was copied by hand or printed from carved wooden blocks. A skilled scribe might need months to produce a single copy of a long work, and books were therefore rare and expensive. Around 1450, Johannes Gutenberg, working in the German city of Mainz, combined several existing technologies into a new system. Individual letters were cast in metal, arranged into lines, inked and pressed onto paper by a screw press similar to those used for making wine. Once a page had been printed, the letters could be taken apart and reused for the next one. Movable type itself was not new; printers in China and Korea had used it before him. What made Gutenberg's system so influential was the way its parts worked together, helped by Europe's alphabet of only a few dozen letters, which made casting a full set of type practical. Within fifty years, printing shops had opened in more than two hundred European towns, and millions of books had been produced. Texts that once existed in a handful of copies now circulated widely, identical from one copy to the next. Scholars in distant cities could study the same edition, compare notes and correct errors, which helped knowledge to accumulate faster than ever before.

er-s005.x: A honeybee that discovers a rich patch of flowers does not keep the news to herself. Back in the dark hive, she performs a 'waggle dance' on the vertical surface of the honeycomb. She runs a short straight line while shaking her body from side to side, then circles back to the start and repeats the run, sometimes dozens of times. In the 1940s the Austrian scientist Karl von Frisch showed that this dance is a kind of map. The angle of the straight run, measured from the vertical, matches the angle between the direction of the food and the direction of the sun. A run pointing straight up the comb means 'fly towards the sun'; a run tilted to the right means the food lies to the right of the sun. The length of each waggle run indicates distance: the longer the run lasts, the farther away the flowers are. Other bees crowd around the dancer, follow her movements and then leave to search in the direction she has shown. Von Frisch's conclusions were challenged at first, because many scientists doubted that an insect could communicate abstract information. Later experiments, including studies with robotic bees that performed the dance themselves, supported his view, and in 1973 he shared the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.

er-s006.x: Economists like to say that nothing is truly free. The idea behind the remark is opportunity cost: the value of the best alternative you give up when you make a choice. Suppose Sana has a free Saturday. She could work at her uncle's shop for a day's wage, revise for her examinations or spend the day with friends. If she chooses to revise, the opportunity cost of that day is not all the other options added together but only the one she would otherwise have chosen, perhaps the wage from the shop. Opportunity cost explains decisions that look puzzling at first. A free concert ticket still costs the hours spent travelling and listening, hours that could have been used for something else. A city that spends money on a new road cannot spend the same money on a hospital or a school. Even a farmer who grows wheat on his own land pays an opportunity cost, since the field could instead have grown cotton or been rented out. The concept does not tell anyone what to choose. People value things differently, and the best alternative for one person may be worthless to another. What it does is encourage a more honest comparison, reminding decision-makers to look not only at the money they spend but also at what they quietly give up.

er-s007.x: The highest mountains on Earth are, in geological terms, still being built. About fifty million years ago, the Indian plate, a vast slab of the Earth's crust that had been drifting northwards across an ancient ocean, began to collide with the Eurasian plate. Neither plate could sink easily beneath the other, because both carried thick, relatively light continental crust. Instead, the rock between them crumpled, folded and was pushed upwards, forming the Himalaya and the neighbouring Karakoram. The collision has not ended. The Indian plate continues to push north by a few centimetres a year, and parts of the Himalaya are still rising by several millimetres annually. Erosion by rivers, glaciers and landslides wears the peaks down, so their height reflects a contest between uplift from below and destruction from above. The same forces explain why northern Pakistan, India and Nepal experience frequent earthquakes. As the plates press against each other, stress builds up along cracks in the rock, called faults, until it is suddenly released. Evidence of the ancient ocean survives in surprising places: fossils of sea creatures have been found in limestone high in the mountains, thousands of metres above today's sea level.

er-s008.t: Why cities stay hot at night
er-s008.x: On a summer evening, the centre of a large city such as Lahore can be several degrees warmer than the farmland around it. This difference is known as the urban heat island effect. Its main causes lie in the materials of the city itself. Asphalt roads, concrete buildings and dark rooftops absorb sunlight during the day and release the stored heat slowly after sunset, so cities cool down far less at night than open countryside does. Air conditioners, vehicles and factories add further heat, and tall buildings packed closely together block the breezes that might carry it away. Vegetation has the opposite effect. Trees shade the ground and, through their leaves, release water vapour that cools the surrounding air as it evaporates. Areas where trees and green spaces have been replaced by pavement therefore tend to be among the hottest parts of a city. The consequences are not only uncomfortable. Hotter nights give people's bodies less chance to recover from daytime heat, which increases health risks for the elderly and for outdoor workers during heatwaves. Higher temperatures also raise the demand for electricity to run fans and air conditioners. Planting trees, protecting parks and painting roofs in light, reflective colours are among the simplest ways to reduce the effect.

er-s009.t: Al-Khwarizmi and the method of steps
er-s009.x: In the early ninth century, Baghdad was home to the House of Wisdom, a centre of learning where scholars translated Greek, Persian and Indian works into Arabic and added discoveries of their own. One of its most influential members was Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi, a mathematician and astronomer whose family probably came from Khwarazm, a region south of the Aral Sea in Central Asia. Around 820 he wrote a book explaining how to solve practical problems of trade, inheritance and land measurement by systematic methods. Its title included the Arabic word al-jabr, meaning 'restoring', which referred to an operation for rearranging the terms of an equation. Through later Latin translations, this word gave European languages the name 'algebra'. Another of his works explained the Hindu-Arabic numerals, including a symbol for zero, and showed how calculations could be carried out with them. When this book was translated into Latin, his name was written as 'Algoritmi', the origin of the modern word 'algorithm'. What made al-Khwarizmi important was less any single result than his approach. Instead of solving each problem by a special trick, he grouped problems into types and gave step-by-step procedures that worked for every case of a type. That idea, a clear set of steps that always leads to an answer, lies at the heart of computer programming today.

er-s010.x: When doctors test a new medicine, it is not enough to give it to sick people and see whether they get better. Many illnesses improve on their own, and patients who expect to recover often report feeling better even when they have received a pill containing nothing but sugar. This response to an inactive treatment is called the placebo effect. It is especially strong for symptoms such as pain and tiredness, which depend partly on how a person feels. To separate the real effect of a drug from these other influences, researchers use controlled trials. Volunteers are divided at random into two groups: one receives the new drug and the other a placebo that looks identical. Random division matters because it makes the groups similar in age, health and other factors, so that any difference in results can be traced to the drug. In the best trials, neither the volunteers nor the doctors treating them know who is receiving which pill until the study ends. Such a trial is called double-blind. If doctors knew, they might, without meaning to, encourage some patients more than others or judge their symptoms differently. Only when the drug group does clearly better than the placebo group do researchers conclude that the medicine works.

er-s011.x: Few sights on Pakistan's highways are as cheerful as a decorated lorry. Known around the world as truck art, the tradition turns ordinary goods vehicles into moving galleries. Every available surface is covered: painted panels show peacocks, flowers, mountain landscapes and portraits, while chains and small metal pendants hang from the bumpers and jingle as the vehicle moves. Lines of poetry or proverbs are often painted along the back. The work is done in specialist workshops in cities such as Karachi, Rawalpindi and Peshawar. A truck may spend several weeks there, passing through the hands of carpenters, metalworkers and painters, each a master of one stage. Many artists learnt the craft as apprentices, watching and assisting older painters for years before being trusted with a panel of their own. Regional styles differ, and experienced observers can often tell from the decoration where a truck was painted. For drivers who spend weeks on the road, the decoration is far more than ornament. A beautifully painted truck reflects the pride of its owner and is, in a sense, a home away from home. In recent decades the style has also moved beyond vehicles. Artists now paint furniture, kettles and shop signs in the same bright manner, and exhibitions abroad have introduced it to new audiences.

er-s012.x: The mountains of northern Pakistan hold thousands of glaciers, among them some of the longest found anywhere outside the polar regions. Siachen, Biafo and Baltoro each stretch for more than fifty kilometres. Together these rivers of ice act as a giant water tower: snow that falls in winter is stored as ice and released as meltwater in summer, feeding the Indus and its tributaries just when farms on the plains need water most. As average temperatures rise, many glaciers in the wider Himalayan region are thinning and retreating. Melting can form lakes at a glacier's edge, held back by loose heaps of rock and ice that the glacier left behind. Such natural dams are weak. If one gives way, perhaps after a sudden ice fall or a spell of very heavy melting, the lake can empty in a few hours. The resulting rush of water, mud and boulders, known as a glacial lake outburst flood, can sweep away bridges, roads and fields far down the valley. Communities in Gilgit-Baltistan and Chitral have begun to prepare. Some valleys now have sensors that measure lake levels and early-warning systems that sound alarms, giving villagers time to move to higher ground. Mapping which lakes are growing fastest helps decide where such equipment is most needed.

er-s013.x: Making dahi at home is one of the oldest uses of biotechnology. Milk is first heated, which kills most unwanted microbes, and then cooled until it is warm but not hot. A spoonful of yesterday's yogurt is stirred in, and the pot is covered and left in a warm place for several hours. By morning, the liquid milk has become a thick, slightly sour curd. The change is the work of bacteria. The starter spoonful contains lactic acid bacteria, which feed on lactose, the natural sugar in milk, and convert it into lactic acid. As acid builds up, the milk becomes more acidic, and its main proteins, which normally float freely, unfold and link together into a soft network that traps the liquid. This is why yogurt sets into a solid mass and why it tastes sour. Temperature controls the process closely. If the milk is too hot when the starter is added, the bacteria die; if it is too cold, they multiply so slowly that the milk may spoil before it sets. This explains the common household advice to wait until the milk feels comfortably warm to a fingertip. The acid also protects the yogurt, since many of the microbes that spoil food cannot grow in such sour conditions, which is why dahi keeps longer than fresh milk.

er-s014.x: When people say that prices have gone up, economists describe the change as inflation: a general rise in the prices of goods and services over time. Inflation does not mean that every price rises equally, or that a single item has become expensive. It means that, on average, the same amount of money buys less than it did before. If inflation is ten per cent a year, a basket of goods that cost 1,000 rupees last year costs about 1,100 rupees today. To measure inflation, statistics offices track the prices of hundreds of items that typical households buy, such as flour, cooking oil, rent, electricity and transport. Each item is weighted according to how much of a household budget it usually takes, so a rise in the price of flour counts for more than a rise in the price of ice cream. The result is a price index, whose change from one year to the next gives the inflation rate. Moderate, steady inflation is considered normal in most economies. Rapid inflation is harmful, because wages and savings often fail to keep pace. A family whose income rises by five per cent while prices rise by twelve per cent is worse off, even though it earns more rupees than before. For this reason economists often compare real incomes, which are adjusted for changes in prices.

er-s015.x: For much of history, sleep was regarded as little more than a pause, a time when the tired brain simply switched off. Research over recent decades has changed that picture. Sleep, it now appears, plays an active part in learning. In a typical experiment, volunteers learn a list of word pairs and are tested twelve hours later. Those who learned in the evening and slept during the interval usually remember more than those who learned in the morning and stayed awake all day, even though the same amount of time has passed. Recordings of brain activity offer a possible explanation. During deep sleep, patterns of activity linked to newly learned material seem to be replayed, and scientists believe this helps move memories from a temporary store in a structure called the hippocampus to more lasting storage in the cortex, the brain's outer layer. Sleep seems to matter before learning as well as after it. People who have been kept awake for a whole night generally find it harder to take in new information the next day, as if the temporary store had not been cleared. These findings carry a practical message for students. Staying up all night before an examination may add a few hours of reading, but it can weaken both the memory of what was studied and the ability to think clearly in the examination hall the next morning.

er-s016.x: Nearly all the water on Earth is in the oceans, but it is far too salty to drink or to use on crops. Desalination plants remove the salt. The older method imitates the natural water cycle: seawater is boiled, and the steam, which leaves the salt behind, is cooled into fresh water. Boiling large volumes of water, however, takes enormous amounts of fuel. Most modern plants use reverse osmosis instead. Seawater is pumped at high pressure against a membrane whose pores are so small that water molecules can pass through but dissolved salts cannot. Fresh water collects on the other side, while a concentrated salty liquid called brine is left behind. Although reverse osmosis needs far less energy than boiling, it still requires powerful pumps, and the membranes must be cleaned or replaced regularly because algae and mineral deposits block them. For coastal cities that suffer water shortages, such as Karachi, desalination is an attractive option because the sea will never run dry. Yet it brings problems of its own. The water it produces costs more than water from rivers or wells, mainly because of the electricity used. The brine must also be disposed of carefully: released in one place, the very salty water can harm sea life near the outlet. Engineers therefore spread the discharge over a wide area or dilute it before it returns to the sea.

er-s017.x: Until the nineteenth century, every town kept its own time. Clocks were set by the sun, so that noon was the moment when the sun stood highest in the sky. Because the Earth turns from west to east, noon arrives earlier in eastern places than in western ones, and towns only a few dozen kilometres apart kept slightly different times. For people who travelled by horse, the difference hardly mattered. The railways changed this. A train could cross a country in hours, and its timetable had to make sense at every station. If each stop used its own local time, a schedule became confusing and, on single-track lines, even dangerous, since two trains might be sent towards each other in the belief that the line was clear. In the 1840s, British railway companies began to adopt a single standard time for all their stations, based on the clock at the Royal Observatory in Greenwich. Within a few decades most of Britain had followed. Larger countries faced a harder problem, since one time could not suit places thousands of kilometres apart. In 1884 an international conference in Washington chose Greenwich as the starting line for measuring longitude, and over the following decades most countries adopted time zones roughly fifteen degrees of longitude wide, usually one hour apart. Pakistan today uses a single zone, five hours ahead of Greenwich.

er-s018.x: About 4,500 years ago, on the banks of the Indus in what is now Sindh, stood one of the largest cities of the ancient world. Mohenjo-daro, as it is called today, may have housed tens of thousands of people. What most impresses visitors is not grand palaces, for none have been found, but the careful planning of ordinary life. The main streets ran roughly north to south and east to west, dividing the city into blocks. Houses were built of baked bricks of standard proportions, and many had their own bathing areas and wells. Waste water flowed from the houses into covered drains along the streets, which had openings at intervals so that they could be cleaned. On a raised mound stood the building known as the Great Bath, a large brick tank made watertight with a layer of natural tar. Its exact purpose is unknown. The people of the Indus civilisation used a script found on thousands of small seals, but no one has yet been able to read it, so much of what we know comes from buildings and objects rather than written records. Since its excavation in the 1920s, the site has suffered from salt rising through the soil and attacking the ancient bricks. It was named a World Heritage Site in 1980, and conservation work continues.

er-s019.x: Water hyacinth is a floating plant with glossy leaves and attractive lilac flowers. It is native to the Amazon basin in South America, but during the nineteenth and twentieth centuries people carried it to gardens and ponds around the world for its beauty. Escaping into rivers, lakes and canals, it has since become one of the most troublesome water weeds on several continents, including parts of South Asia. The plant's success comes from its speed. Under warm conditions it can double the area it covers in a couple of weeks, spreading both by seed and by sending out runners that grow into new plants. Outside its native range, it also lacks the insects and diseases that keep it in check at home. A thick mat of hyacinth causes many problems. It blocks sunlight from the water below, so underwater plants die, and their decay uses up oxygen that fish need. The mats clog irrigation channels and the intakes of pumps, hinder boats and fishing nets, and provide still water in which mosquitoes breed. Removing the plant by hand or machine is costly and must be repeated, because small fragments soon regrow. Some countries have had success with biological control: releasing weevils from the plant's native region that feed only on water hyacinth. Others try to make use of the harvested plant, turning it into compost, animal feed or woven baskets.

er-s020.t: Ibn al-Haytham and the path of light
er-s020.x: How do we see? Many ancient thinkers believed that the eye sends out invisible rays that touch objects, rather as a hand feels its way in the dark. In the early eleventh century, the scholar Ibn al-Haytham, who was born in Basra and did much of his work in Cairo, set out to test such ideas by careful observation and experiment. In his Book of Optics, he argued that vision happens the other way round: light travels in straight lines from objects into the eye. He pointed out, for example, that looking at the sun hurts the eyes, which is hard to explain if the eye only sends rays out. To study how light behaves, he used a darkened room with a tiny hole in one wall. Light from the bright scene outside passed through the hole and formed an upside-down image on the opposite wall, an arrangement later known as the camera obscura. Just as important as his conclusions was his method. Ibn al-Haytham insisted that claims should be checked against controlled experiments, that measurements should be repeated, and that a scholar should examine even respected authorities critically. His book was translated into Latin and studied for centuries by European scientists, and many historians regard him as an early pioneer of the experimental approach on which modern science depends.

er-s021.x: Pakistan receives strong sunshine for much of the year, and rooftop solar panels have become a common sight in its cities and villages. A solar panel is made of cells, usually of silicon, that convert light directly into electricity. When light strikes a cell, it gives energy to electrons in the silicon, and a built-in electric field pushes those electrons through a circuit as a current. There are no moving parts, which is one reason panels can last for twenty years or more. The amount of electricity a panel produces depends on more than the brightness of the sky. Panels work best when they face the sun directly, so in Pakistan, which lies north of the equator, fixed panels are usually tilted towards the south. Dust is another enemy. A layer of fine dust blocks part of the light, and in dry, dusty regions panels that are not cleaned can lose a noticeable share of their output within weeks. Surprisingly, heat is a problem too. Although panels need sunlight, their cells become less efficient as they get hotter, so a panel on a scorching June afternoon in Multan may produce less than the same panel on a bright but cool day in spring. Installers therefore leave a gap beneath the panels so that air can flow and carry heat away.

er-s022.x: Plastic does not rot in the way that wood or paper does. Instead, sunlight, waves and friction slowly break larger items, such as bags and bottles, into smaller and smaller pieces. Fragments less than five millimetres across are called microplastics. Some are made small on purpose, such as the tiny beads once common in face scrubs, and others are fibres that wash out of synthetic clothes in washing machines. Because they are so small and light, microplastics travel far. Scientists have found them in deep ocean sediments, in Arctic sea ice, in river water and in the air of cities. Sea creatures from tiny plankton to large fish swallow them, often mistaking them for food, and in this way the particles can pass along food chains. What microplastics do to living things is still being studied. In laboratory experiments, some animals that ate large amounts grew more slowly or ate less real food, because their stomachs were partly filled. The particles can also carry chemicals that stick to their surfaces. Researchers stress, however, that the effects on human health are not yet well understood. Since microplastics are almost impossible to collect once they are spread through the environment, most experts argue that the most effective response is to stop plastic waste from reaching rivers and seas in the first place.

er-s023.x: Imagine a farmer who has wheat and wants shoes. In a world without money, he must find a shoemaker who not only has shoes to spare but also happens to want wheat. Economists call this requirement a double coincidence of wants, and it makes barter, the direct exchange of goods, slow and awkward. A shoemaker who wants rice instead might refuse, and the farmer would have to arrange a chain of trades to get what he needs. Money solves this problem by acting as a medium of exchange: something everyone accepts in payment, not because they want it for itself but because they know others will accept it in turn. The farmer can sell his wheat to anyone who wants it and use the money to buy shoes from anyone who has them. Money also serves two other purposes. It is a unit of account, a common measure that lets people compare the values of very different things, from a bag of flour to a bicycle. It is also a store of value, since, unlike wheat, which may spoil, money can be saved for later use. Over history, many objects have served as money, including shells, salt, cattle and metal coins. Today most money exists only as numbers in bank records, yet it works because people trust that it will be accepted tomorrow.

er-s024.x: Every winter, a grey haze settles over Lahore and much of the Punjab plains, at times so thick that flights are delayed and motorways are closed. This smog is a mixture of smoke, dust and gases from many sources: vehicle exhaust, factories, brick kilns, the burning of rubbish and, in some weeks, the burning of crop stubble in fields after the rice harvest. These sources produce pollution all year round, so why is winter so much worse? Part of the answer lies in the weather. Normally, air near the ground is warmer than the air above it. Warm air rises, carrying pollutants upwards where they spread out and thin. On calm winter nights, however, the ground cools quickly, and the air touching it becomes colder than the layer above. This situation is called a temperature inversion. The warm layer acts like a lid: the cold, polluted air beneath cannot rise, and with little wind to blow it away, the pollution builds up day after day. Smog irritates the eyes and throat and can worsen asthma and other lung diseases, especially in children and the elderly. Doctors advise people to limit time outdoors on the worst days. Lasting improvement, though, depends on reducing what goes into the air: cleaner fuels and engines, modern kilns and alternatives to burning crop residue.

er-s025.x: Science is often pictured as the work of experts in laboratories, but some of the most useful data today are collected by ordinary people. In citizen science projects, volunteers record observations that professional researchers could never gather alone. Thousands of birdwatchers count the species in their gardens on the same weekend each year; schoolchildren measure rainfall; amateur astronomers scan the night sky for new comets and exploding stars. The strength of such projects lies in numbers and spread. A single research team might survey a few sites in detail, while volunteers can cover an entire country and keep doing so year after year. Over time, their records reveal patterns, such as birds arriving earlier in spring or a butterfly spreading into new regions, that would otherwise go unnoticed. Critics once worried that data from untrained observers would be unreliable. Project designers have responded in several ways. They give clear instructions and simple identification guides, ask volunteers to upload photographs that experts can check, and use computer programs to flag records that look unusual, such as a tropical bird reported in a snowy region. Studies comparing volunteer and expert data have often found them broadly similar for common, easily recognised species, though less so for rare or confusing ones. Mobile phones have made taking part easier than ever. With a camera and an app, almost anyone can contribute to real research.

er-q001.x: A large share of the rubbish thrown away by a typical Pakistani household, often around half, is food and garden waste: vegetable peels, tea leaves, eggshells, fallen leaves and grass cuttings. When this material is buried in a landfill site, it is squeezed together with plastic and other waste, cut off from air, and slowly broken down by microbes that do not need oxygen. That process releases methane, a gas that traps far more heat in the atmosphere than carbon dioxide does. Composting offers a better route. In a compost heap or bin, the same waste is broken down by microbes that do need oxygen, helped by worms, insects and fungi. A good heap mixes ‘green’ materials, which are moist and rich in nitrogen, such as peels and fresh grass, with ‘brown’ materials, which are dry and rich in carbon, such as dead leaves, straw and torn cardboard. It should be kept about as damp as a squeezed sponge and turned every week or two to let in air. If it smells bad, it is usually too wet or has too much green material, and adding browns and turning it solves the problem. As the microbes work, the centre of the heap becomes warm. After two to six months, the waste becomes a dark, crumbly material that smells of soil. Mixed into a garden or into pots, it improves the soil's structure, helps it hold water and returns nutrients to plants.

er-q002.x: Archaeologists excavating ancient Egyptian tombs are reported to have found pots of honey that were thousands of years old and still showed no sign of rotting. Few natural foods keep so well, and the reasons lie in honey's chemistry. Bees make honey from nectar, a thin, sugary liquid. In the hive they add an enzyme to it and fan it with their wings until most of the water evaporates, leaving a thick syrup that is about four-fifths sugar and less than a fifth water. Bacteria and moulds need water to grow, and honey contains so much sugar that it draws water out of any microbe that lands in it, leaving the microbe unable to multiply. Honey is also fairly acidic, which makes it even harder for most microbes to survive. In addition, the enzyme the bees add slowly produces small amounts of hydrogen peroxide, a substance that kills many germs. These defences work only while honey stays thick. If it absorbs water, for example when it is stored in an open jar in a damp kitchen or when a wet spoon is dipped into it, yeasts can begin to ferment it. Honey that turns grainy or solid has not spoiled; it has simply crystallised, as the sugar comes out of solution, and gentle warming will make it runny again. Honey should not be given to babies under one year old, because it can carry bacterial spores that a baby's gut cannot yet resist.

er-q003.x: Twice a day, on most coasts, the sea slowly rises up the shore and then falls back. These tides are caused mainly by the Moon's gravity. The Moon pulls on the whole Earth, but its pull is strongest on the side of the Earth that faces it and weakest on the far side. As a result, the ocean on the near side is drawn towards the Moon, forming a bulge, and a second bulge forms on the far side, where the water is pulled less strongly than the solid Earth and is in effect left behind. As the Earth turns, a given coast passes through both bulges, which is why most places have two high tides and two low tides in a little more than a day. The Sun also raises tides, though its effect is a little less than half that of the Moon, because it is so much farther away. When the Sun, Moon and Earth lie in a line, at new moon and full moon, their effects combine to produce spring tides, with especially high high tides and low low tides. When the Sun and Moon pull at right angles, at the quarter moons, the tides are weaker and are called neap tides. Despite the name, spring tides have nothing to do with the season; they occur about twice every month throughout the year. The shape of the coast also matters: in narrow bays the tidal range can be many metres, while in some enclosed seas it is very small.

er-q004.t: A theory that takes a risk
er-q004.x: How can we tell a scientific theory from a claim that only sounds scientific? In the twentieth century, the philosopher Karl Popper offered an influential answer. A theory is scientific, he argued, only if it is falsifiable: it must forbid certain things from happening, so that an observation could in principle show it to be false. Consider the statement ‘all swans are white’. No number of white swans can prove it, since the next swan might be black, but a single black swan would disprove it. For Popper, this imbalance was the key to science. Scientists should not hunt for observations that agree with their theories, which are easy to find, but should design tests that could prove them wrong. A theory that survives many serious attempts at refutation earns our confidence, though never final certainty. By contrast, a claim that can be made to fit any possible outcome tells us nothing. A fortune-teller who predicts that ‘something important will happen to you soon’ can never be shown wrong, and that is exactly the weakness of the prediction. Popper's view has been criticised. Real scientists do not abandon a well-supported theory the moment one result disagrees with it; they first check the equipment, repeat the experiment and consider other explanations. Even so, his central idea remains widely taught: a good theory takes a risk by saying clearly what should not happen.

er-q005.x: The desert locust is a kind of grasshopper that lives in the dry lands stretching from West Africa to India and Pakistan. For most of the time, it leads a quiet, solitary life. Individual locusts are green or brown, avoid one another and do little damage. Everything changes after unusually heavy rains. Plants spring up, the locusts breed rapidly, and when the vegetation dries out again the young insects are forced together on the remaining patches of green. Crowding sets off a remarkable transformation. Repeated touching of their hind legs triggers chemical changes in the locusts' nervous system, and within a few hours they start to seek each other out instead of avoiding one another. Over the following weeks and generations, they change colour to yellow and black, develop stronger flight muscles and begin to move in huge bands and then swarms. A large swarm can contain many millions of insects, travel more than a hundred kilometres in a day with the wind, and eat roughly its own weight in crops and pasture every day. Because swarms cross many borders, control depends on cooperation between countries. Survey teams watch breeding areas after rains, and satellite data on rainfall and vegetation help them predict where outbreaks might begin. Stopping a swarm early, before it grows, is far cheaper and more effective than fighting it once it has spread.

er-q006.x: For more than two thousand years, travellers, traders and armies have moved along a great route across the north of the subcontinent, linking the plains of Bengal with Lahore, Peshawar and, beyond the Khyber Pass, Kabul. Today it is known as the Grand Trunk Road, and in Pakistan much of its course is followed by the national highway N-5. The road owes much of its shape to Sher Shah Suri, who ruled northern India for a few years in the 1540s. In that short time he had a long stretch of it rebuilt and extended. Along the way he ordered the construction of sarais, roadside inns where travellers could rest and find water and food, at regular intervals. Trees were planted for shade, wells were dug, and tall brick pillars known as kos minars marked distances. Messengers on horseback could change to fresh horses at the sarais, so news travelled far faster than before. Later rulers maintained the road, and in the nineteenth century it was resurfaced and given the name by which it is known today. The road did more than carry goods. Because people of many regions met and mixed along it, it spread languages, foods, crafts and ideas. Writers have often described it as a river of life, and even today a journey along it passes through a long chain of towns that grew up beside it.

er-q007.x: Chess is played today in almost every country, but its earliest known form, called chaturanga, appeared in India around the sixth century. Its pieces represented the four divisions of an ancient army: foot soldiers, horsemen, elephants and chariots, led by a king and his chief adviser. From India the game travelled to Persia, where it was known as shatranj. The Persian phrase shah mat, roughly ‘the king is helpless’, is the source of the English word checkmate. The game was later taken up across the Arab world, where players wrote books analysing positions and composed puzzles, and from there it reached Europe through Spain and Italy around the tenth century. For several hundred years the rules stayed close to the Persian ones, and games were slow. The adviser could move only one square diagonally, and the elephant could jump just two squares, so the pieces took a long time to meet. Then, at the end of the fifteenth century, players in southern Europe made a dramatic change. The adviser became the queen and gained the power to move any distance in any direction, and the elephant's successor could sweep along whole diagonals. Attacks became faster and more dangerous, and the modern game was born. Chess has continued to change in other ways. In 1997 a computer, Deep Blue, defeated the world champion Garry Kasparov in a match, and today almost every serious player trains with chess programs.

er-q008.x: In the 1790s, the Italian scientist Lazzaro Spallanzani carried out a puzzling experiment. Bats that could not see still flew easily around obstacles in a dark room, but bats whose ears were blocked blundered into walls. Spallanzani concluded that bats somehow ‘see’ with their ears, yet he could not explain how, since he heard nothing. The answer came in the late 1930s, when the American researcher Donald Griffin used new equipment that could detect sounds too high for human ears. He found that flying bats give out a rapid series of high-pitched calls and listen for the echoes. He named the method echolocation. An echo carries a great deal of information. The time it takes to return tells the bat how far away an object is, and small differences between the sound reaching its two ears tell it the direction. As a bat closes in on an insect, it calls faster and faster, up to about two hundred times a second, so that it can follow every turn of its prey. Not all bats hunt this way; many large fruit-eating bats rely mainly on their eyes and sense of smell. The insects have not been idle either. Some moths can hear bat calls and drop suddenly towards the ground when one approaches, and a few produce clicks of their own that seem to confuse the hunter.

er-q009.x: In the Salt Range of northern Punjab, near the town of Khewra in Jhelum District, lies one of the oldest and largest salt mines in the world. The salt there formed hundreds of millions of years ago, when an ancient sea dried up and left thick beds of minerals that were later buried and pushed upwards by movements of the Earth's crust. Much of Khewra's rock salt is pink or reddish, a colour that comes from small traces of other minerals, especially iron; purer layers are white or clear. Salt has been dug here for many centuries, but the mine's modern layout dates from 1872, when a British mining engineer planned its main tunnels. Khewra is worked by the room-and-pillar method. Miners cut out large chambers but leave about half the salt standing as thick columns that hold up the roof. This wastes a great deal of salt, yet it is far safer than removing everything, because salt can slowly creep and flow under heavy pressure. Galleries run for many kilometres and descend through several levels inside the mountain. Today Khewra is also one of Pakistan's best-known tourist sites. Visitors ride a small train into the mountain to see illuminated chambers, a pool of brine and models built from blocks of salt. The same salt that once went mainly to kitchens and cattle is now sold worldwide in decorative lamps and as coarse pink table salt.

er-q010.x: On a long bus journey or a flight, the steady roar of an engine can be tiring even when it is not especially loud. Noise-cancelling headphones reduce such sound by adding more sound. The idea depends on the fact that sound is a wave of tiny pressure changes in the air. When two waves meet, they combine. If the high-pressure part of one wave arrives at the same moment as the low-pressure part of another wave of the same size, the two cancel out and the result is near silence. This effect is called destructive interference. In noise-cancelling headphones, small microphones on the outside of each ear cup pick up the surrounding noise. Electronic circuits then produce a matching wave that is exactly reversed, sometimes called anti-noise, and the headphone speaker plays it together with the music. The approach works best on steady, low-pitched sounds such as the hum of an engine or an air conditioner, because these change slowly and are easy to predict. Sudden or high-pitched sounds, such as a baby crying or people talking nearby, change too quickly to be cancelled fully; for these, the headphones rely mostly on the cushions that seal around the ears and block sound in the ordinary way. The basic principle was patented in the 1930s, but it became practical only with small, fast electronics, and it was first widely used in headsets for pilots.

questions.s: Choose the word closest in meaning to: ABUNDANT
questions.e: ABUNDANT means existing in large quantities, so PLENTIFUL is the match. SCARCE is the opposite (in short supply), and ABRUPT (sudden) only begins with the same letters.

questions.s: Choose the word closest in meaning to: METICULOUS
questions.e: METICULOUS means showing great care over every small detail, which is what PAINSTAKING means. RECKLESS (careless of danger) is close to the opposite, and neither TALKATIVE nor FEARFUL has anything to do with care.

questions.s: Choose the word closest in meaning to: HOSTILE
questions.e: HOSTILE means showing dislike or opposition, i.e. UNFRIENDLY. HOSPITABLE looks similar but means welcoming to guests, the opposite idea.

questions.s: In the sentence "The old typewriter became OBSOLETE once computers arrived in every office.", the word OBSOLETE most nearly means
questions.e: OBSOLETE means no longer used because something newer has replaced it, so OUTDATED fits. EXPENSIVE may sound plausible for an old machine, but it describes price, not being out of use.

questions.s: Choose the word closest in meaning to: CANDID
questions.e: CANDID means honest and direct in what one says, i.e. FRANK. SUGARY is a trap from its likeness to "candy", and GUARDED (careful not to reveal much) is nearly the opposite.

questions.s: Choose the word closest in meaning to: OBSEQUIOUS
questions.e: OBSEQUIOUS means too eager to please or obey, i.e. SERVILE. OBSTINATE (stubborn, refusing to give way) shares the opening letters but describes the reverse attitude, and OBVIOUS is only a look-alike.

questions.s: Choose the word closest in meaning to: BENEVOLENT
questions.e: BENEVOLENT means well-meaning and kindly, so KIND-HEARTED is the synonym. VIOLENT is suggested by the ending "-volent", but it means using force to harm, the opposite of benevolent.

questions.s: Choose the word closest in meaning to: FRAGILE
questions.e: FRAGILE means easily broken or damaged, i.e. DELICATE. STURDY is the opposite, and FRAGRANT (sweet-smelling) only looks similar.

questions.s: In the sentence "Ayesha's explanation was so LUCID that even the youngest students understood it.", the word LUCID most nearly means
questions.e: LUCID means expressed clearly and easy to understand, so CLEAR fits; the sentence says even young students understood it. LENGTHY describes length, not clarity, and LUCKY is only a look-alike.

questions.s: Choose the word closest in meaning to: EPHEMERAL
questions.e: EPHEMERAL means lasting for a very short time, i.e. SHORT-LIVED. ETHEREAL sounds similar but means light, delicate or heavenly, and ETERNAL (lasting for ever) is the opposite.

questions.s: Choose the word closest in meaning to: DILIGENT
questions.e: DILIGENT means showing steady care and effort in one's work, i.e. HARD-WORKING. INTELLIGENT rhymes with it and is often linked with good students, but it means clever, not industrious; LAZY is the opposite.

questions.s: Choose the word closest in meaning to: RAPID
questions.e: RAPID means happening or moving very quickly, i.e. SWIFT. SLOW is the opposite, and RIGID (stiff) only looks alike.

questions.s: Choose the word closest in meaning to: PRUDENT
questions.e: PRUDENT means acting with care and good judgement for the future, i.e. SENSIBLE. PROUD only shares its first letters, and RASH (acting without thinking) is the opposite.

questions.s: Choose the word closest in meaning to: ADVERSITY
questions.e: ADVERSITY means a difficult or unlucky situation, i.e. HARDSHIP. ADVANTAGE looks similar but means a favourable condition, which is nearly the opposite.

questions.s: In the sentence "The minister's speech was full of PLATITUDES that said nothing new.", the word PLATITUDES most nearly means
questions.e: A PLATITUDE is a remark used so often that it is dull and meaningless, i.e. a CLICHÉ, which matches "said nothing new". COMPLIMENTS are expressions of praise; a speech can be full of them and still be original.

questions.s: Choose the word closest in meaning to: VACANT
questions.e: VACANT means not occupied or filled, i.e. EMPTY. BUSY is the opposite, while VALIANT (brave) and VAGUE (unclear) only begin with the same letter.

questions.s: Choose the word closest in meaning to: TENACIOUS
questions.e: TENACIOUS means holding firmly to a purpose and not giving up, i.e. PERSISTENT. TENSE (nervous, stretched tight) only looks similar, and TIMID (shy, easily frightened) suggests giving up easily.

questions.s: Choose the word closest in meaning to: PERFUNCTORY
questions.e: PERFUNCTORY means done quickly as a routine, with little care or interest, i.e. CURSORY. THOROUGH is the opposite, and PUNCTUAL (on time) is a trap because both describe how a duty is carried out.

questions.s: Choose the word closest in meaning to: CONCISE
questions.e: CONCISE means giving much information in few words, i.e. BRIEF. PRECISE looks and sounds similar but means exact or accurate; a long answer can be precise without being concise.

questions.s: In the sentence "Hamza was ELATED when he heard that he had passed his exams.", the word ELATED most nearly means
questions.e: ELATED means extremely happy and excited, i.e. OVERJOYED, which suits passing exams. RELATED only rhymes with it and means connected, and WORRIED is the opposite feeling.

questions.s: Choose the word closest in meaning to: AMBIGUOUS
questions.e: AMBIGUOUS means open to more than one meaning and so not clear, i.e. UNCLEAR. AMBITIOUS looks alike but means eager to succeed, and OBVIOUS is the opposite.

questions.s: Choose the word closest in meaning to: LACONIC
questions.e: LACONIC means using very few words, i.e. TERSE. TALKATIVE is the opposite, and LAZY is a trap because laconic people may seem to make little effort, but the word is about speech, not work.

questions.s: Choose the word closest in meaning to: GENUINE
questions.e: GENUINE means truly what it is said to be, i.e. REAL. FAKE is the opposite, while GENEROUS and GENTLE only share the opening letters.

questions.s: Choose the word closest in meaning to: SCRUTINISE
questions.e: SCRUTINISE means to examine something closely and carefully, i.e. INSPECT. IGNORE is the opposite, and SCRIBBLE (write carelessly) only begins with the same letters.

questions.s: In the sentence "The villagers were RELUCTANT to leave their homes despite the flood warning.", the word RELUCTANT most nearly means
questions.e: RELUCTANT means not wanting to do something, i.e. UNWILLING. RELIEVED (freed from worry) only looks similar, and EAGER is the opposite.

questions.s: Choose the word closest in meaning to: TRIVIAL
questions.e: TRIVIAL means of little value or importance, i.e. UNIMPORTANT. SERIOUS is the opposite, and TRIBAL (to do with a tribe) only looks similar.

questions.s: Choose the word closest in meaning to: DOCILE
questions.e: DOCILE means quiet and easily controlled or taught, i.e. OBEDIENT. REBELLIOUS is the opposite, and FERTILE shares only the "-ile" ending.

questions.s: Choose the word closest in meaning to: AUDACIOUS
questions.e: AUDACIOUS means willing to take bold risks, i.e. DARING. CAUTIOUS is the opposite, and AUDIBLE (loud enough to be heard) only shares the opening letters.

questions.s: In the sentence "Living on a small salary, Bilal had to be FRUGAL with every rupee.", the word FRUGAL most nearly means
questions.e: FRUGAL means careful not to spend more money than needed, i.e. THRIFTY, which fits a small salary. FRUITFUL looks alike but means productive, and GENEROUS is the opposite of frugal.

questions.s: Choose the word closest in meaning to: MUNDANE
questions.e: MUNDANE means dull and everyday, lacking excitement, i.e. ORDINARY. THRILLING is the opposite, and MANDATORY (compulsory) only looks similar.

questions.s: Choose the word closest in meaning to: VIGILANT
questions.e: VIGILANT means keeping careful watch for danger, i.e. WATCHFUL. CARELESS is the opposite, and VIOLENT only shares the opening letters.

questions.s: Choose the word closest in meaning to: ERRATIC
questions.e: ERRATIC means not even or regular in pattern, unpredictable, i.e. IRREGULAR. STEADY is the opposite, and ENERGETIC is a trap because erratic movement can look lively, but energetic means full of energy, not uneven.

questions.s: Choose the word closest in meaning to: COPIOUS
questions.e: COPIOUS means abundant, in large amounts, i.e. PROFUSE ("copious notes", "profuse thanks"). MEAGRE is the opposite, and PRECIOUS (of great value) describes worth, not quantity.

questions.s: In the sentence "Climbing to the base camp of K2 is an ARDUOUS journey that takes many days.", the word ARDUOUS most nearly means
questions.e: ARDUOUS means needing great effort and endurance, i.e. STRENUOUS. ARDENT looks similar but means passionate or eager, which describes a person's feelings, not a journey.

questions.s: Choose the word closest in meaning to: BELLIGERENT
questions.e: BELLIGERENT means hostile and eager to fight or argue, i.e. AGGRESSIVE. PEACEFUL is the opposite, and ELEGANT (graceful) has a similar sound but no link in meaning.

questions.s: Choose the word closest in meaning to: INNATE
questions.e: INNATE means present in a person from birth rather than acquired, i.e. INBORN. LEARNED (gained by study) is the opposite, and ORNATE (richly decorated) only rhymes.

questions.s: Choose the word closest in meaning to: LETHARGIC
questions.e: LETHARGIC means lacking energy and slow, i.e. SLUGGISH. ENERGETIC is the opposite, and LETHAL (deadly) only shares the opening letters.

questions.s: Choose the word closest in meaning to: ZEAL
questions.e: ZEAL means great energy or eagerness for a cause, i.e. ENTHUSIASM. JEALOUSY is a trap because "zealous" and "jealous" look alike, but jealousy is resentment of another's success; BOREDOM is the opposite.

questions.s: In the sentence "The dark clouds suggested that a storm was IMMINENT.", the word IMMINENT most nearly means
questions.e: IMMINENT means about to happen very soon, i.e. IMPENDING. EMINENT is a common confusion but means famous and respected, and DISTANT is the opposite.

questions.s: Choose the word closest in meaning to: DIMINISH
questions.e: DIMINISH means to become or make smaller, i.e. DECREASE. INCREASE is the opposite, and FINISH only shares the ending.

questions.s: Choose the word closest in meaning to: HAUGHTY
questions.e: HAUGHTY means proud and looking down on others, i.e. ARROGANT. HUMBLE is the opposite, and NAUGHTY (badly behaved) only rhymes.

questions.s: Choose the word closest in meaning to: AMIABLE
questions.e: AMIABLE means pleasant and good-natured, i.e. FRIENDLY. AMUSING (funny) also describes pleasant company, but a person can be amiable without being funny; RUDE is the opposite.

questions.s: Choose the word closest in meaning to: INDIGENOUS
questions.e: INDIGENOUS means originating naturally in a place, i.e. NATIVE. POOR is a trap from the look-alike word "indigent" (needy), and FOREIGN is the opposite.

questions.s: Choose the word closest in meaning to: CONSPICUOUS
questions.e: CONSPICUOUS means easily seen or attracting attention, i.e. NOTICEABLE. HIDDEN is the opposite, and SUSPICIOUS only sounds alike.

questions.s: Choose the word closest in meaning to: PRAGMATIC
questions.e: PRAGMATIC means dealing with things sensibly, based on what works in practice, i.e. PRACTICAL. IDEALISTIC (guided by ideals rather than reality) is close to the opposite, and DRAMATIC only rhymes.

questions.s: Choose the word closest in meaning to: ESOTERIC
questions.e: ESOTERIC means understood by only a few people with special knowledge, i.e. ARCANE. POPULAR (liked or known by many) is the opposite, and EXTERIOR is a trap from the ending "-teric", but it means outside.

questions.s: In the sentence "Unlike his shy brother, Usman is GREGARIOUS and loves big family gatherings.", the word GREGARIOUS most nearly means
questions.e: GREGARIOUS means fond of company, i.e. SOCIABLE, which fits "loves big family gatherings". GRACIOUS looks alike but means courteous and kind, and SOLITARY (preferring to be alone) is the opposite.

questions.s: Choose the word closest in meaning to: ALLEVIATE
questions.e: ALLEVIATE means to make pain or a problem less severe, i.e. RELIEVE. WORSEN is the opposite, and ELEVATE (raise up) only looks similar.

questions.s: Choose the word closest in meaning to: CURTAIL
questions.e: CURTAIL means to cut short or limit, i.e. REDUCE. EXTEND is the opposite, and COVER is a trap from "curtain", which is a different word.

questions.s: In the sentence "The judge remained IMPARTIAL and listened carefully to both sides.", the word IMPARTIAL most nearly means
questions.e: IMPARTIAL means treating all sides equally, i.e. UNBIASED, which fits listening to both sides. INCOMPLETE is a trap from reading "impartial" as "not whole", and PREJUDICED is the opposite.

questions.s: Choose the word closest in meaning to: TIMID
questions.e: TIMID means lacking courage or confidence, i.e. SHY. BOLD is the opposite, and TIDY and TIMELY only look similar.

questions.s: Choose the word closest in meaning to: DREAD
questions.e: DREAD means great fear of something that may happen, i.e. FEAR. COURAGE is the opposite, and DREAM only looks alike.

questions.s: Choose the word closest in meaning to: OBSTACLE
questions.e: An OBSTACLE is something that blocks the way, i.e. a BARRIER. HELP is the opposite, and SPECTACLE (an impressive sight) only shares the ending "-tacle".

questions.s: Choose the word closest in meaning to: VIVID
questions.e: VIVID means producing strong, bright colours or clear images, i.e. BRIGHT. DULL is the opposite, while VALID (acceptable) and VITAL (essential) only look similar.

questions.s: Choose the word closest in meaning to: HUMID
