questions.e: An introductory infinitive phrase ('To get a place at NUST') must be followed by the person who wants the place. Only 'Hamza began preparing' supplies that subject. 'Hamza's preparation began' makes 'preparation' the subject, and preparation cannot get a university place: a dangling modifier.

questions.s: Choose the correct sentence.
o: A boy wearing a red cap was chased by a dog.
A boy was chased by a dog wearing a red cap.
Wearing a red cap, a dog chased a boy.
A dog chased, wearing a red cap, a boy.
questions.e: The modifier 'wearing a red cap' must sit next to the noun it describes, the boy. In 'chased by a dog wearing a red cap' the phrase is next to 'dog', so the dog seems to wear the cap. Putting the phrase at the start makes it describe 'a dog' too.

questions.s: Choose the best replacement for the part in capitals: THE TEACHER RETURNED THE TESTS TO THE STUDENTS THAT SHE HAD MARKED.
o: The teacher returned the tests to the students that she had marked.
The teacher returned the tests that she had marked to the students.
The teacher, that she had marked, returned the tests to the students.
That she had marked, the teacher returned the tests to the students.
questions.e: A relative clause should follow the noun it describes. The teacher marked the tests, so 'that she had marked' must come straight after 'tests'. In the original it follows 'students', which says she marked the students: a misplaced modifier.

questions.s: Choose the best replacement for the part in capitals: BEING A RAINY DAY, the match was postponed.
o: As it was a rainy day,
questions.e: 'Being a rainy day' has no subject of its own, so it attaches to 'the match', and a match cannot be a rainy day: a dangling participle. A clause with its own subject, 'As it was a rainy day,', fixes this. 'Having been a rainy day' has the same fault and also the wrong time sense.

questions.s: Choose the correct sentence.
o: Having lost his ticket, the conductor made Ali pay again.
Having lost his ticket, Ali's fare had to be paid again.
Having lost his ticket, Ali had to pay the conductor again.
Having lost his ticket, a second fare was charged to Ali.
questions.e: The opening participle phrase 'Having lost his ticket' refers to the subject after the comma, so that subject must be the person who lost the ticket, Ali. In the first sentence the conductor seems to have lost it; in the others 'fare' is the subject, which is a dangling modifier.

questions.s: Choose the best replacement for the part in capitals: ON REACHING THE STATION, THE TRAIN HAD ALREADY LEFT.
o: On reaching the station, we found that the train had already left.
On reaching the station, the train had already left.
On reaching the station, the train was found to have left already by us.
Reaching the station, the train had already left us.
questions.e: 'On reaching the station' needs as its subject the people who reached it. The original makes 'the train' that subject, which is illogical because the train had left. Only 'we found that the train had already left' gives the phrase the right subject; the passive 'was found ... by us' still leaves 'the train' as subject.

questions.s: Choose the correct sentence.
o: Hamza saw a herd of deer driving along the motorway.
Driving along the motorway, Hamza saw a herd of deer.
A herd of deer, driving along the motorway, Hamza saw.
Hamza, a herd of deer, saw driving along the motorway.
questions.e: The modifier 'driving along the motorway' describes Hamza, so it must sit next to 'Hamza'. In the first sentence it follows 'deer', so the deer appear to be driving: a misplaced modifier. The last two jumble the word order and are ungrammatical.

questions.s: Choose the best replacement for the part in capitals: HOPING TO WIN THE PRIZE, A NEW STRATEGY WAS TRIED BY THE TEAM.
o: Hoping to win the prize, a new strategy was tried by the team.
Hoping to win the prize, there was a new strategy tried by the team.
Hoping to win the prize, the team's new strategy was tried.
Hoping to win the prize, the team tried a new strategy.
questions.e: The participle phrase 'Hoping to win the prize' must be followed by the subject who hopes, the team. Changing to the active voice, 'the team tried a new strategy', does this. In the original the subject is 'a new strategy', and a strategy cannot hope, so the modifier dangles; 'the team's new strategy' has the same fault.

questions.s: Fatima answered 18 of the 20 questions correctly. Which sentence describes this correctly?
o: Fatima got all the answers almost right.
Almost Fatima got all the answers right.
Fatima got almost all the answers right.
Fatima got all the almost answers right.
questions.e: 'Almost' modifies the word it stands before. To say she got most but not every answer right, it must come before 'all': 'almost all the answers'. 'All the answers almost right' says every answer was nearly but not quite correct, which is a different meaning; the other two are ungrammatical.

questions.s: Identify the error in the sentence: Sana likes (A) reading novels, (B) writing poems and (C) to paint (D) landscapes.
questions.e: Items joined in a list must have the same grammatical form (parallelism). 'Reading' and 'writing' are gerunds, so the third item must be 'painting', not the infinitive 'to paint'. The other marked parts are correct.

questions.s: Choose the correct sentence.
o: Ali not only plays cricket but also hockey.
Ali plays not only cricket but also hockey.
Not only Ali plays cricket but also hockey.
Ali plays not only cricket but also he plays hockey.
questions.e: With 'not only ... but also', the words after each part must be parallel. In 'plays not only cricket but also hockey' both parts are followed by a noun. In 'not only plays cricket but also hockey' a verb phrase is paired with a bare noun, so the pair is unbalanced.

questions.s: Choose the best replacement for the part in capitals: The new principal is efficient, honest and HAS A LOT OF KINDNESS.
questions.e: After 'is', the list 'efficient, honest and ...' is a series of adjectives, so the last item must be an adjective too: 'kind'. 'A kind person' is a noun phrase and 'has a lot of kindness' is a verb phrase, so both break the parallel structure.

questions.s: Identify the error in the sentence: (A) To swim, (B) cycling and (C) jogging (D) are all good forms of exercise.
questions.e: The three subjects in the list must be parallel. 'Cycling' and 'jogging' are gerunds, so the first must be 'Swimming', not the infinitive 'To swim'. 'Are' is correct because the compound subject is plural.

questions.s: Choose the correct sentence.
o: The scheme is both good for farmers and for traders.
The scheme both is good for farmers and traders.
Both the scheme is good for farmers and for traders.
The scheme is good both for farmers and for traders.
questions.e: 'Both' and 'and' must be followed by matching structures. In 'good both for farmers and for traders' each is followed by a phrase starting 'for'. In 'both good for farmers and for traders', 'both' comes before an adjective but 'and' before a preposition, so the pair is not parallel.

questions.s: Choose the best replacement for the part in capitals: The job requires ATTENTION TO DETAIL, PATIENCE AND THAT YOU CAN WORK UNDER PRESSURE.
o: attention to detail, patience and that you can work under pressure
attention to detail, patience and the ability to work under pressure
attention to detail, being patient and to work under pressure
being attentive to detail, patience and working under pressure
questions.e: The objects of 'requires' form a list and must all be noun phrases: 'attention', 'patience' and 'the ability'. A 'that' clause cannot sit in a list of nouns. The other options mix gerunds, infinitives and nouns, so they are not parallel.

questions.s: Identify the error in the sentence: The report was clear, (A) concise and (B) it was well organised, (C) so the board (D) approved it.
questions.e: 'Clear, concise and ...' is a list of adjectives after 'was', so the last item must be the adjective phrase 'well organised', not the clause 'it was well organised'. The rest of the sentence is correct.

questions.s: Choose the correct sentence.
o: The fan neither cools the room nor does it reduce the noise.
Neither the fan cools the room nor reduces the noise.
The fan neither cools the room nor reduces the noise.
The fan cools neither the room nor reduces the noise.
questions.e: 'Neither' and 'nor' must each be followed by the same kind of element. In 'neither cools the room nor reduces the noise' both are followed by a verb phrase. 'Nor does it reduce' switches to a clause, and 'cools neither the room nor reduces' pairs a noun with a verb.

questions.s: Choose the best replacement for the part in capitals: In the holidays Usman likes to read, to swim and GOING HIKING.
questions.e: The list after 'likes' begins with the infinitives 'to read' and 'to swim', so the last item must also be an infinitive: 'to hike'. 'Going hiking' is a gerund phrase and breaks the parallel structure.

questions.s: Identify the error in the sentence: A good essay has (A) a clear thesis, (B) strong evidence, (C) careful structure and (D) it uses simple language.
questions.e: The objects of 'has' form a list of noun phrases, so the last item must be a noun phrase too: 'simple language'. The clause 'it uses simple language' breaks the parallel structure. The first three parts are correct.

questions.s: Choose the correct sentence.
o: It is easier to plan a project than to carry it out.
It is easier to plan a project than carrying it out.
Planning a project is easier than to carry it out.
To plan a project is easier than carrying it out.
questions.e: The two things compared must have the same form. 'To plan' is compared with 'to carry it out', two infinitives. The other options compare an infinitive with a gerund, or a gerund with an infinitive, which breaks parallelism.

questions.s: Choose the best replacement for the part in capitals: Ayesha spoke CLEARLY, CONFIDENT AND WITH HUMOUR.
questions.e: All three words describe how she spoke, so they must all be adverbs: 'clearly, confidently and humorously'. 'Confident' and 'humorous' are adjectives and cannot modify the verb 'spoke', and mixing them with adverbs also breaks parallelism.

questions.s: Identify the error in the sentence: This (A) mango is (B) more sweeter (C) than the one (D) we bought yesterday.
questions.e: A comparative is formed either with -er or with 'more', never both. 'Sweet' is a short adjective, so the comparative is 'sweeter'; 'more sweeter' is a double comparative. The other marked parts are correct.

questions.s: Choose the best replacement for the part in capitals: The climate of Murree is cooler THAN LAHORE.
questions.e: Comparisons must compare like with like. The sentence compares the climate of Murree with the climate of Lahore, so the singular pronoun 'that' must stand for 'the climate': 'than that of Lahore'. 'Than Lahore' compares a climate with a city, and 'those' is plural, so it cannot replace 'climate'.

questions.s: Identify the error in the sentence: Hamza is (A) as tall (B) like (C) his (D) father.
questions.e: An equal comparison is made with 'as ... as': 'Hamza is as tall as his father.' The second 'as' cannot be replaced by 'like'. 'As tall' is the correct first half of the pattern.

questions.s: Choose the correct sentence.
o: Karachi is larger than any city in Pakistan.
Karachi is largest than any other city in Pakistan.
Karachi is the larger city than any in Pakistan.
Karachi is larger than any other city in Pakistan.
questions.e: When something is compared with the rest of its own group, 'other' is needed: Karachi is itself a city in Pakistan, so it is larger than 'any other city'. Without 'other' the sentence says Karachi is larger than itself. 'Largest than' wrongly mixes a superlative with 'than'.

questions.s: Choose the best replacement for the part in capitals: Of the two sisters, Zainab is THE TALLEST.
questions.e: When exactly two people or things are compared, the comparative degree is used: 'the taller of the two'. The superlative 'the tallest' is kept for three or more. 'More taller' is a double comparative.

questions.s: Choose the correct sentence.
o: Usman's handwriting is neater than his brother's.
Usman's handwriting is neater than his brother.
Usman's handwriting is more neater than his brother's.
Usman's handwriting is neater than his brother is.
questions.e: Handwriting must be compared with handwriting, so the possessive 'his brother's' (meaning his brother's handwriting) is needed. 'Neater than his brother' and 'than his brother is' compare handwriting with a person. 'More neater' is a double comparative.

questions.s: Identify the error in the sentence: Sana is (A) the (B) most cleverest (C) student (D) in the class.
questions.e: A superlative is formed with -est or with 'most', never both. 'Most cleverest' is a double superlative; the correct form is 'cleverest' (or 'most clever'). The article 'the' before a superlative is correct.

questions.s: Choose the best replacement for the part in capitals: Hamza runs AS FAST AS, IF NOT FASTER THAN, his cousin.
o: as fast as, if not faster than,
as fast, if not faster than,
as fast as, if not faster,
so fast as, if not faster than,
questions.e: The sentence must read correctly with either comparison alone: 'Hamza runs as fast as his cousin' and 'Hamza runs faster than his cousin'. So both 'as' and 'than' are needed. Dropping the second 'as' gives 'as fast his cousin', and dropping 'than' gives 'faster his cousin'.

questions.s: Identify the error in the sentence: Mr Khan is (A) senior (B) than all the other (C) teachers (D) in the school.
questions.e: 'Senior' is one of the Latin comparatives (senior, junior, superior, inferior, prior) that take 'to' instead of 'than': 'senior to all the other teachers'. 'All the other teachers' is correct because Mr Khan is himself a teacher in the school.

questions.s: Choose the best replacement for the part in capitals: There were LESS STUDENTS in the hall than last year.
questions.e: 'Fewer' is the comparative used with countable plural nouns such as students; 'less' is used with uncountable nouns (less water, less time). 'Few' is not a comparative and cannot be followed by 'than', and 'lesser' means smaller in importance.

questions.s: Choose the correct sentence.
o: The roads of Islamabad are wider than most other cities.
The roads of Islamabad are wider than that of most other cities.
The roads of Islamabad are wider than those of most other cities.
The roads of Islamabad are more wider than those of other cities.
questions.e: Roads must be compared with roads, not with cities, so a pronoun standing for 'the roads' is needed. Because 'roads' is plural, the pronoun is 'those': 'than those of most other cities'. 'That of' is singular and does not agree with 'roads'; 'more wider' is a double comparative.

questions.s: Choose the correct sentence.
o: This year's results are more good than last year's.
This year's results are gooder than last year's.
This year's results are best than last year's.
This year's results are better than last year's.
questions.e: 'Good' has irregular degrees: good, better, best. The comparative 'better' is used with 'than'. 'More good' and 'gooder' are not standard, and the superlative 'best' cannot be followed by 'than'.

questions.s: Identify the error in the sentence: If it (A) will rain tomorrow, (B) the match (C) will be (D) cancelled.
questions.e: In a first conditional the if-clause takes the present simple and the main clause takes 'will': 'If it rains tomorrow, the match will be cancelled.' 'Will' does not go in the if-clause to show future time, so 'will rain' is the error.

questions.s: Choose the best replacement for the part in capitals: If you had told me earlier, I WOULD HELP you.
questions.e: The if-clause 'had told' (past perfect) shows an unreal past situation, which is a third conditional. Its main clause needs 'would have' + past participle: 'I would have helped you'. 'Would help' belongs to the second conditional, which talks about the present or future.

questions.s: Choose the correct sentence.
o: If I have a car, I would drive you to the airport.
If I would have a car, I would drive you to the airport.
If I had a car, I would drive you to the airport.
If I had a car, I will drive you to the airport.
questions.e: For an imaginary present situation (I do not have a car), the second conditional uses the past simple in the if-clause and 'would' + base verb in the main clause. 'Have ... would' and 'had ... will' mix two conditional types, and 'would' is not used in the if-clause.

questions.s: Choose the best replacement for the part in capitals: IF I WOULD HAVE KNOWN about the traffic, I would have left earlier.
questions.e: This is a third conditional about the past, so the if-clause needs the past perfect: 'If I had known', which can be inverted to 'Had I known'. 'Would have' never goes in the if-clause, and 'If I knew' is the second-conditional form, which does not match 'would have left'.

questions.s: Choose the correct sentence.
o: If you heat ice, it melts.
If you heat ice, it melted.
If you will heat ice, it melts.
If you heated ice, it melts.
questions.e: A general scientific truth uses the zero conditional: present simple in both clauses, 'If you heat ice, it melts.' The other options mix tenses: a past tense in one clause with a present in the other, or 'will' inside the if-clause.

questions.s: Identify the error in the sentence: (A) Unless you (B) do not submit the form (C) by Friday, you (D) will lose your place.
questions.e: 'Unless' already means 'if not', so it is followed by a positive verb: 'Unless you submit the form by Friday'. Adding 'do not' makes a double negative and reverses the meaning. The main clause with 'will' is correct for a first conditional.

questions.s: Choose the correct sentence.
o: If Bilal caught the bus, he would not have been late now.
If Bilal had caught the bus, he would not be late now.
If Bilal had caught the bus, he will not be late now.
If Bilal would have caught the bus, he would not be late now.
questions.e: This is a mixed conditional: an unreal past condition (had caught) with a present result (would not be late now). The word 'now' needs 'would' + base verb in the main clause. 'Will' is wrong for an unreal result, and 'would have' never goes in the if-clause.

questions.s: Identify the error in the sentence: If Sana (A) knew the answer, (B) she (C) will tell (D) us at once.
questions.e: The past simple 'knew' in the if-clause marks a second conditional (an imaginary present). Its main clause needs 'would' + base verb: 'she would tell us at once'. 'Will tell' belongs to the first conditional and does not match 'knew'.

questions.s: Choose the best replacement for the part in capitals: If the driver HAD NOT BRAKED in time, the car would have hit the child.
questions.e: The main clause 'would have hit' shows a third conditional about an unreal past event. The if-clause therefore needs the past perfect: 'had not braked'. 'Did not brake' is the second-conditional form, and 'would not have' cannot be used in the if-clause.

questions.s: Choose the correct sentence.
o: Should you needed any help, please call me.
Should you will need any help, please call me.
Should you need any help, please call me.
If should you need any help, please call me.
questions.e: 'Should' can replace 'if' at the start of a conditional by inversion: 'Should you need help' means 'If you need help'. Like any modal, 'should' is followed by the base form 'need', not 'needed'. Inversion replaces 'if', so 'If should' is wrong.

questions.s: Choose the best replacement for the part in capitals: If Fatima leaves now, she WOULD CATCH the five o'clock train.
questions.e: 'If Fatima leaves now' uses the present simple for a real possibility, so this is a first conditional. The main clause takes 'will' + base verb: 'she will catch the train'. 'Would catch' belongs to the second conditional and needs a past tense in the if-clause.

questions.s: Identify the error in the sentence: If the team (A) had practised more, they (B) would (C) win (D) the final last week.
questions.e: The past perfect 'had practised' shows a third conditional about the past (the final has already been played). The main clause needs 'would have' + past participle: 'would have won'. So 'win' is the error; 'had practised' is correct.

questions.s: Choose the correct passive form of: The workers are building a new bridge.
o: A new bridge is being built by the workers.
A new bridge is built by the workers.
A new bridge was being built by the workers.
A new bridge has been built by the workers.
questions.e: The present continuous passive is am/is/are + being + past participle. 'Are building' therefore becomes 'is being built', with 'is' agreeing with 'a new bridge'. 'Is built' is the present simple passive, and 'was being built' changes the tense to the past.

questions.s: Choose the correct passive form of: Who wrote this letter?
o: By whom this letter was written?
By whom was this letter wrote?
By whom was this letter written?
questions.e: In the passive, 'who' as subject becomes 'by whom', and a question keeps the auxiliary before the subject: 'By whom was this letter written?' The passive needs the past participle 'written', not the past tense 'wrote'. 'By whom this letter was written?' uses statement word order in a question.

questions.s: Identify the error in the sentence: The thief (A) was (B) catch (C) by the police (D) last night.
questions.e: The passive voice is formed with a form of 'be' plus the past participle. The past participle of 'catch' is 'caught', so the sentence should read 'was caught by the police'. 'Was' is correct for a past simple passive.

questions.s: Choose the correct passive form of: Ayesha has completed the project.
o: The project has completed by Ayesha.
The project had been completed by Ayesha.
The project has been completed by Ayesha.
The project was being completed by Ayesha.
questions.e: The present perfect passive is has/have + been + past participle, so 'has completed' becomes 'has been completed'. Leaving out 'been' gives an active verb with the wrong meaning, and 'had been' or 'was being' change the tense.

questions.s: Choose the best replacement for the part in capitals: The forms MUST SUBMIT before Monday.
questions.e: The forms do not submit anything; they are submitted, so the passive is needed. A modal passive is modal + be + past participle: 'must be submitted'. 'Must been' leaves out 'be', and 'must have submit' uses the wrong verb form.

questions.s: Choose the correct passive form of: Close the door.
questions.e: An imperative sentence is made passive with 'Let' + object + be + past participle: 'Let the door be closed.' After 'let' the bare form 'be' is required, so 'Let the door is closed' is wrong, and 'The door be closed' has no 'let' to begin the command.

questions.s: Choose the correct sentence.
o: The accident was happened on the motorway.
The accident has been happened on the motorway.
The accident had been happen on the motorway.
The accident happened on the motorway.
questions.e: 'Happen' is an intransitive verb: it takes no object, so it cannot be put into the passive voice. The correct form is the simple active 'The accident happened'. Forms such as 'was happened' and 'has been happened' are common errors.

questions.s: Choose the correct passive form of: People say that he is honest.
o: He is said to be honest.
He is said that he is honest.
He is saying to be honest.
questions.e: With reporting verbs such as say, believe and think, the passive can be made with the person as subject followed by an infinitive: 'He is said to be honest.' 'He is said that he is honest' repeats the subject and keeps a that-clause, and 'He said to be honest' drops the auxiliary 'is', so it is no longer passive.

questions.s: Identify the error in the sentence: When the lights went out, the patient (A) was (B) being (C) examine (D) by the doctor.
questions.e: The past continuous passive is was/were + being + past participle. The participle of 'examine' is 'examined', so the verb should be 'was being examined'. 'Was' and 'being' are both correct here.

questions.s: Choose the correct active form of: The match was won by our team.
o: Our team has won the match.
Our team had won the match.
questions.e: 'Was won' is the past simple passive, so the active form keeps the past simple: 'Our team won the match.' The agent 'our team' becomes the subject. 'Has won', 'wins' and 'had won' change the tense.

questions.s: Choose the correct passive form of: Did Usman break the window?
o: Did the window broken by Usman?
Was the window broken by Usman?
Was the window broke by Usman?
Has the window been broken by Usman?
questions.e: A past simple question with 'did' becomes 'was/were' + subject + past participle in the passive: 'Was the window broken by Usman?' The passive needs the participle 'broken', not the past tense 'broke'. 'Has ... been broken' changes the tense to the present perfect.

questions.s: Choose the correct indirect form of: Ali said, "I am tired."
o: Ali said that I am tired.
Ali said that he had been tired.
Ali said that he was tired.
Ali told that he was tired.
questions.e: With a past reporting verb the present simple moves back to the past simple (am → was) and the pronoun changes to match the speaker (I → he). 'Had been' moves the tense back too far, and 'told' must be followed by the listener, as in 'told me'.

questions.s: Choose the correct indirect form of: The teacher said to Hamza, "Where do you live?"
o: The teacher asked Hamza where he lived.
The teacher asked Hamza where did he live.
The teacher asked Hamza where does he live.
The teacher said to Hamza where he lived.
questions.e: A reported question uses 'asked' and the word order of a statement: subject before verb, with no 'do/does/did'. 'Do you live' therefore becomes 'he lived'. 'Where did he live' keeps question word order, and 'said to' is not used to report a question.

questions.s: Choose the correct indirect form of: The doctor said to Sana, "Take this medicine twice a day."
o: The doctor told Sana that take this medicine twice a day.
The doctor told Sana to take that medicine twice a day.
The doctor said Sana to take that medicine twice a day.
The doctor told to Sana to take that medicine twice a day.
questions.e: A command is reported with told/ordered/advised + listener + to-infinitive, and 'this' becomes 'that'. 'Said Sana to take' is wrong because 'say' cannot take the listener directly, and 'told to Sana' wrongly adds 'to' after 'told'.

questions.s: Identify the error in the sentence: Fatima (A) asked me (B) whether (C) had I (D) finished my work.
questions.e: In a reported yes/no question, 'whether' or 'if' is followed by normal statement order: subject then verb. So 'had I finished' must be 'I had finished'. 'Asked me whether' is the correct way to report the question.

questions.s: Choose the correct indirect form of: Bilal said, "I will come tomorrow."
o: Bilal said that I would come the next day.
Bilal said that he would came the next day.
Bilal told that he would come the next day.
Bilal said that he would come the next day.
questions.e: In indirect speech 'will' becomes 'would', 'I' becomes 'he' for the speaker, and 'tomorrow' becomes 'the next day'. A modal is followed by the base form 'come', not 'came', and 'told' needs a listener after it.

questions.s: Choose the correct indirect form of: Zainab said, "I lost my purse yesterday."
o: Zainab said that she has lost her purse the day before.
Zainab said that she had lost her purse the day before.
Zainab said that she had lost my purse the previous day.
Zainab said that she was lose her purse the day before.
questions.e: After 'said', the past simple 'lost' moves back to the past perfect 'had lost', 'my' becomes 'her', and 'yesterday' becomes 'the day before'. 'Has lost' does not move the tense back, and keeping 'my' makes the purse belong to the reporter.

questions.s: Choose the correct indirect form of: Usman said, "What a beautiful view!"
o: Usman exclaimed that what a beautiful view it was.
Usman said that what a beautiful view!
Usman exclaimed that it was a very beautiful view.
Usman exclaimed what a beautiful view is it.
questions.e: An exclamation is reported with a verb such as 'exclaimed' and turned into a statement: 'What a beautiful view!' becomes 'that it was a very beautiful view'. 'That what' joins two introducers, and 'is it' keeps question order and the present tense.

questions.s: Identify the error in the sentence: Hamza (A) said me (B) that he (C) had passed (D) his driving test.
questions.e: 'Say' cannot be followed directly by the listener; use 'told me' or 'said to me'. In indirect speech the usual form is 'Hamza told me that he had passed his driving test'. The past perfect 'had passed' is correct after a past reporting verb.

questions.s: Choose the correct direct form of: She asked me if I was coming to the party.
o: She said to me, "Was I coming to the party?"
She said to me, "Am I coming to the party?"
She said to me, "Are you came to the party?"
She said to me, "Are you coming to the party?"
questions.e: Going back to direct speech, the tense moves forward (was coming → are coming), the listener 'I' becomes 'you', and question word order returns. 'Am I coming' keeps the reporter's pronoun, and 'are you came' uses the wrong verb form.

questions.s: Choose the correct indirect form of: The guard said to us, "Do not park here."
o: The guard told us not to park there.
The guard told us not park there.
The guard told us do not park there.
The guard told us that not to park there.
questions.e: A negative command is reported with told + listener + 'not to' + base verb, and 'here' becomes 'there'. Leaving out 'to' or keeping 'do not' is wrong, and 'that' cannot introduce an infinitive.

questions.s: Choose the correct indirect form of: Sana said, "I am writing this essay now."
o: Sana said that she had written that essay then.
Sana said that I was writing that essay then.
Sana said that she was writing that essay then.
Sana said that she was write that essay then.
questions.e: After 'said', the present continuous becomes the past continuous (am writing → was writing), 'I' becomes 'she', 'this' becomes 'that' and 'now' becomes 'then'. 'Had written' changes the meaning to a finished action, and 'I' keeps the wrong pronoun.

questions.s: Identify the error in the sentence: The officer asked Bilal (A) what (B) was his name (C) and where (D) he worked.
questions.e: A reported question takes statement order: 'what his name was', with the subject before the verb. The second question, 'where he worked', already has the correct order, which shows the fault in the first. 'Was his name' keeps the inverted order of a direct question.

questions.s: Choose the best replacement for the part in capitals: Reading a book is often more rewarding THAN TO WATCH a film.
questions.e: The two things compared must have the same form. The subject is the gerund 'Reading', so the second item must be the gerund 'watching'. 'To watch' is an infinitive and breaks parallelism; 'having watched' changes the time sense.

questions.s: Choose the best replacement for the part in capitals: WHILE CROSSING THE BRIDGE, A BEAUTIFUL SUNSET WAS SEEN.
o: While crossing the bridge, a beautiful sunset was seen.
While crossing the bridge, a beautiful sunset was seen by us.
While crossing the bridge, there was a beautiful sunset.
While crossing the bridge, we saw a beautiful sunset.
questions.e: 'While crossing the bridge' must be followed by the people who were crossing. In the passive versions the subject is 'a beautiful sunset', so the sunset seems to cross the bridge, even when 'by us' is added. The active 'we saw a beautiful sunset' fixes the dangling modifier.

questions.s: Choose the best replacement for the part in capitals: I would have bought the shoes IF I HAD HAD enough money.
questions.e: The main clause 'would have bought' is a third conditional, so the if-clause needs the past perfect of 'have', which is 'had had'. The sentence is correct as it stands. 'Would have' is never used in the if-clause, and 'have had' or 'will have' do not show an unreal past.

questions.s: Choose the best replacement for the part in capitals: Ayesha asked me WHAT TIME DID THE SHOP OPEN.
o: what time did the shop open
what time does the shop open
that what time the shop opened
questions.e: Reported questions use statement order with no 'do/does/did': 'what time the shop opened'. The past 'opened' follows the past reporting verb 'asked'. 'That what' wrongly adds 'that' before a question word.

questions.s: Choose the best replacement for the part in capitals: LIKE MANY OTHER STUDENTS, HAMZA'S AMBITION IS to study engineering.
o: Like many other students, Hamza has the ambition
Like many other students, Hamza's ambition is
Like many other students, Hamza's ambition was
Similar to many other students, Hamza's ambition is
questions.e: A comparison must compare like with like. 'Like many other students' compares people, so the word after the comma must be a person: 'Hamza has the ambition'. In the original, students are compared with an ambition, and changing 'is' to 'was' or 'Like' to 'Similar to' does not remove that fault.

questions.s: Choose the best replacement for the part in capitals: The committee reviewed the plan and IT WAS APPROVED BY THEM.
questions.e: Two actions by the same subject should be joined in the same form and voice: 'reviewed the plan and approved it'. Switching to the passive 'it was approved by them' breaks the parallel structure and is wordy. 'Approving' does not match the past tense 'reviewed'.

questions.s: Choose the best replacement for the part in capitals: If you press this button, the machine STOPPED.
questions.e: A fact about how a machine always works takes the zero conditional: present simple in both clauses, 'If you press this button, the machine stops.' The past forms 'stopped' and 'had stopped' do not match the present 'press', and 'would have stopped' belongs to the third conditional.

questions.s: Choose the correct indirect form of: Ayesha said to her brother, "Please lend me your pen."
o: Ayesha requested her brother to lend me your pen.
Ayesha requested to her brother to lend her his pen.
Ayesha said her brother please to lend her his pen.
Ayesha requested her brother to lend her his pen.
questions.e: A polite request is reported with requested/asked + listener + to-infinitive, and 'please' is dropped. Pronouns change to fit the people: 'me' becomes 'her' and 'your' becomes 'his'. 'Requested to her brother' wrongly adds 'to', and keeping 'me your pen' leaves the direct-speech pronouns.

questions.s: Choose the best replacement for the part in capitals: WHEN ONLY SIX YEARS OLD, Zainab's father taught her to swim.
o: At the age of only six,
When Zainab was only six years old,
questions.e: A shortened clause such as 'When only six years old' takes its subject from the main clause, which is 'Zainab's father', so the father seems to be six. Giving the clause its own subject, 'When Zainab was only six years old,', removes the dangling modifier. 'At the age of only six' and 'Being only six years old' still attach to the father.

questions.s: Each of the students ______ a laptop for the course.
questions.e: 'Each of' + plural noun takes a singular verb because the subject is 'each', not 'students'. So 'Each of the students has'. 'Have' is tempting because 'students' stands next to the verb, but it is only the object of 'of'.

questions.s: Identify the error: The box of old letters (A) were found (B) in the attic (C) by my grandmother (D) last week.
questions.e: The subject is 'The box', which is singular; 'of old letters' only describes it. The verb must agree with the head noun: 'The box ... was found'. The other parts are correct: 'in the attic', 'by my grandmother' (passive agent) and 'last week' with the past tense.

questions.s: Choose the correct sentence.
o: Neither the manager nor his assistants was present at the meeting.
The quality of these mangoes are excellent this year.
Either the students or the teacher is responsible for the noise.
The pictures on the wall was painted by my aunt.
questions.e: With 'either ... or' and 'neither ... nor', the verb agrees with the nearer subject: 'the teacher is'. In the first sentence the nearer subject 'his assistants' is plural, so it needs 'were'. 'The quality ... is' and 'The pictures ... were' follow the head noun, not the noun in the 'of' or 'on' phrase.

questions.s: Mathematics ______ my favourite subject since Class 6.
questions.e: Subjects ending in -ics, such as mathematics and physics, are singular, and 'since Class 6' needs the present perfect. So 'Mathematics has been'. 'Have been' has the right tense but treats 'mathematics' as plural because of the final -s.

questions.s: Identify the error: The teacher, (A) along with her students, (B) are planning (C) a visit (D) to the museum.
questions.e: Phrases such as 'along with', 'as well as' and 'together with' do not change the number of the subject. The subject is 'The teacher', so the verb must be 'is planning'. The plural 'students' inside the commas misleads many readers into choosing 'are'.

questions.s: Choose the correct sentence.
o: There is many books on the shelf.
There are a lot of traffic on the road today.
There is a lot of traffic on the road today.
There are a little milk left in the jug.
questions.e: After 'there is/are' the verb agrees with the noun that follows. 'Traffic' and 'milk' are uncountable and take 'is', while 'books' is plural and takes 'are'. 'A lot of' does not make 'traffic' plural, so 'There are a lot of traffic' is wrong.

questions.s: Bread and butter ______ his usual breakfast.
questions.e: Two nouns joined by 'and' normally take a plural verb, but when they name a single idea or dish, as in 'bread and butter', the verb is singular. Here they form one breakfast, so 'is'. 'Are' applies the general 'and' rule without noticing that the pair is one item.

questions.s: Identify the error: A number of candidates (A) has applied (B) for the post, but (C) only a few (D) will be selected.
questions.e: 'A number of' means 'many' and takes a plural verb: 'A number of candidates have applied'. Do not confuse it with 'The number of', which takes a singular verb ('The number of candidates is large'). 'Only a few' correctly means 'some, but not many'.

questions.s: Choose the correct sentence.
o: The number of road accidents have risen sharply.
The scissors is on the table next to the thread.
The news from the flooded villages is worrying.
questions.e: 'News' is uncountable and always singular, so 'The news ... is' is correct. 'The number of' takes a singular verb ('has risen'), 'mathematics' is singular, and 'scissors' is a plural-only noun that takes 'are'.

questions.s: The police ______ looking into the matter.
questions.e: 'Police' is a plural noun in standard English, like 'cattle' and 'people', so it takes a plural verb: 'The police are looking'. 'Is' and 'was' treat it as a singular group noun, which is a common mistake.

questions.s: Identify the error: Every year many a student (A) from small towns (B) dream (C) of studying (D) at NUST.
questions.e: 'Many a' is followed by a singular noun and a singular verb: 'many a student dreams'. 'From small towns' only describes the student. 'Dream of + -ing' and 'at NUST' are correct.

questions.s: Choose the correct sentence.
o: Physics and chemistry is compulsory for us.
Every boy and girl were given a prize.
The teacher and the students was in the hall.
The boy and his sister have gone to Multan.
questions.e: Two different people or things joined by 'and' take a plural verb, so 'The boy and his sister have gone' is correct, and the first and third sentences should use 'are' and 'were'. When 'every' or 'each' comes before nouns joined by 'and', the verb is singular: 'Every boy and girl was given a prize'.

questions.s: Identify the error: The judges (A) were impressed, and (B) the prize (C) was shared between Ayesha (D) and I.
questions.e: A pronoun that is the object of a preposition takes the object case. 'Between' is a preposition, so it must be 'between Ayesha and me'. Test it by removing 'Ayesha and': nobody would say 'between I'.

questions.s: The children enjoyed ______ at the picnic.
questions.e: The reflexive pronoun for 'they' is 'themselves', used when the object is the same as the subject. 'Theirselves' and 'themself' are non-standard forms, and 'themselfs' misspells the plural of 'self' (selves).

questions.s: This bag is not mine; it must be ______.
questions.e: A possessive pronoun that stands alone, without a noun after it, is 'hers' (like 'mine', 'yours', 'ours'). Possessive pronouns never take an apostrophe, so 'her's' is wrong; 'she's' means 'she is', and 'her' needs a noun after it ('her bag').

questions.s: Identify the error: The company (A) has decided (B) to move (C) it's head office (D) to Lahore.
questions.e: 'It's' is the short form of 'it is' or 'it has'; the possessive pronoun is 'its', with no apostrophe. The sentence needs 'its head office'. 'Has decided' agrees with the singular 'The company'.

questions.s: The officer to ______ you should send the form is on leave.
questions.e: A relative pronoun directly after a preposition takes the object form, so 'to whom'. 'Who' is the subject form and cannot follow 'to'. 'Which' is used for things, not people, and 'whose' needs a noun after it.

questions.s: Choose the correct sentence.
o: We students want a longer break.
The coach gave Hamza and I extra practice.
Him and his brother run a shop in Saddar.
Fatima and myself will host the event.
questions.e: 'We' is the subject form, so 'We students want' is correct (test by dropping 'students': 'We want'). 'Gave Hamza and I' needs the object form 'me', 'Him and his brother' as a subject needs 'He', and a reflexive pronoun cannot be a subject, so 'Fatima and I will host'.

questions.s: I met the doctor ______ son is in my class.
questions.e: 'Whose' is the possessive relative pronoun: the son belongs to the doctor ('the doctor whose son'). 'Who' and 'whom' cannot be followed directly by the noun 'son' in this way, and 'which' refers to things.

questions.s: Identify the error: My brother and (A) me (B) went (C) to the market (D) yesterday.
questions.e: The pronoun is part of the subject, so it needs the subject case: 'My brother and I went'. Remove 'My brother and' to test it: 'me went' is clearly wrong. 'Went' correctly matches 'yesterday'.

questions.s: He has lived in Peshawar ______ 2019.
questions.e: With the present perfect, 'since' is used before a point in time (2019, Monday, March) and 'for' before a length of time (five years). 2019 is a point in time, so 'since'. 'In 2019' would need the simple past ('He moved there in 2019').

questions.s: Identify the error: I (A) have watched (B) that film (C) with my friends (D) at the cinema last Friday.
questions.e: The present perfect is not used with a finished past time such as 'last Friday', 'yesterday' or 'two days ago'. The simple past is needed: 'I watched that film'. 'With my friends' and 'at the cinema' are correct prepositions.

questions.s: By the time we reached the station, the train ______.
questions.e: When one past action was complete before another past action, the earlier one takes the past perfect. The train left before we reached the station, so 'had already left'. 'Has already left' is present perfect and does not fit a story told in the past ('reached').

questions.s: Identify the error: She (A) is knowing (B) the answer, but (C) she is too shy (D) to speak.
questions.e: Stative verbs such as know, believe, understand, own and like are not normally used in the continuous tenses. The sentence needs the simple present: 'She knows the answer'. 'Too shy to speak' is the correct 'too + adjective + to-infinitive' pattern.

questions.s: Look at those dark clouds! It ______ rain.
questions.e: 'Be going to' is used for a prediction based on present evidence, here the dark clouds. So 'It is going to rain'. 'Goes to' and 'is raining to' are not English future forms, and 'will be going rain' is ungrammatical.

questions.s: I will call you when I ______ in Karachi.
questions.e: In a time clause beginning with when, as soon as, until, before or after, the simple present is used for a future action; 'will' goes only in the main clause. So 'I will call you when I arrive'. 'When I will arrive' puts the future in the time clause, which is wrong.

questions.s: Choose the correct sentence.
o: I am living in Quetta since 2020.
The bus left before we have arrived.
She has been working at the bank for six years.
He has finished the report two hours ago.
questions.e: An action that began in the past and still continues takes the present perfect continuous with 'for' or 'since': 'has been working ... for six years'. 'Am living ... since 2020' should be 'have been living', and 'two hours ago' marks a finished past time, so it needs the simple past 'finished'. 'Before we have arrived' should be 'before we arrived'.

questions.s: No sooner had the bell rung ______ the students rushed out.
questions.e: The fixed pattern is 'No sooner + had + subject + past participle ... than + simple past'. So 'No sooner had the bell rung than the students rushed out'. 'When' belongs with 'hardly' and 'scarcely', which is why it is the most tempting wrong choice.

questions.s: Hardly ______ the hall when the lights went out.
questions.e: When a sentence begins with the negative adverb 'Hardly', the subject and auxiliary are inverted, and the earlier action takes the past perfect: 'Hardly had we entered the hall when ...'. 'We had entered' keeps normal word order, and 'did we entered' wrongly uses a past form after 'did'.

questions.s: Identify the error: It (A) has been (B) raining (C) since three hours, (D) so the roads are flooded.
questions.e: 'Three hours' is a length of time, so it takes 'for', not 'since': 'It has been raining for three hours'. 'Since' is used only before a starting point, such as 'since morning' or 'since 6 o'clock'. The present perfect continuous 'has been raining' is correct.

questions.s: While I ______ for the exam, the power went off.
questions.e: A longer action in progress in the past that is interrupted by a short past action takes the past continuous: 'While I was studying ..., the power went off'. 'Am studying' is present and clashes with 'went off', and 'has been studying' does not agree with 'I'.

questions.s: Choose the correct sentence.
o: Water boil at 100 °C at sea level.
The earth moves round the sun.
The sun is rising in the east every day.
Birds is flying south in winter.
questions.e: Facts and general truths take the simple present, with -s for a singular subject: 'The earth moves'. 'Water boil' lacks the -s, and 'is rising ... every day' uses the continuous for a permanent truth. 'Birds is flying' breaks agreement and uses the wrong tense.

questions.s: Identify the error: When I (A) reached the hall, I (B) realised that I (C) left my admit card (D) at home.
questions.e: Leaving the card happened before reaching the hall and realising, so the earlier past action takes the past perfect: 'I had left my admit card at home'. 'Reached' and 'realised' are both simple past because they happen in sequence at the same point in the story.

questions.s: Ayesha ______ her homework yet.
questions.e: In British English, 'yet' in a negative sentence goes with the present perfect, because it means 'up to now': 'has not finished ... yet'. 'Did not finish' is simple past and refers to a finished time, which does not fit 'yet'.

questions.s: Choose the correct sentence.
o: He go to college by bus every day.
They was playing hockey when it began to rain.
We have known each other since childhood.
questions.e: The present perfect with 'since' shows a state that began in the past and continues, and 'have' agrees with 'We'. 'He go' needs 'goes' for a singular subject, 'They was' needs 'were', and 'She have' needs 'has'.

questions.s: Identify the error: Every morning my father (A) is reading (B) the newspaper (C) before he (D) leaves for work.
questions.e: A habit or routine, signalled by 'every morning', takes the simple present: 'my father reads the newspaper'. The present continuous is for actions happening now. 'Leaves' is correctly simple present in the time clause.

questions.s: It is high time we ______ the old wiring in this building.
questions.e: After 'It is (high) time + subject', the verb is in the past tense even though the meaning is present or future: 'It is high time we replaced'. The past form shows that the action is overdue. 'Replace' looks natural because the meaning is present, but it breaks this fixed pattern.

questions.s: She ______ in this school for ten years when she retired last year.
questions.e: The ten years of teaching came before another past point (her retirement), so the past perfect is needed: 'She had taught ... for ten years when she retired'. 'Has taught' is present perfect, which cannot be tied to a past event such as 'last year'.

questions.s: Identify the error: Hamza (A) did not (B) went (C) to the match because he (D) was ill.
questions.e: After the auxiliary 'did' (and 'does', 'do'), the main verb is in the base form: 'did not go'. The past tense is already shown by 'did', so 'went' doubles it. 'Was ill' agrees with 'he' and is in the past tense.

questions.s: Choose the correct sentence.
o: I am waiting here for two hours.
The film had started before we will reach.
We has visited the museum twice.
She was cooking when the guests arrived.
questions.e: An action in progress (was cooking) interrupted by a short past action (arrived) takes the past continuous plus the simple past. 'I am waiting ... for two hours' needs 'I have been waiting', 'We has' needs 'have', and the second sentence wrongly mixes the past perfect with 'will'.

questions.s: In which sentence does every pronoun refer clearly to only one noun?
o: Ayesha told her sister that she had won the prize.
The teacher spoke to Usman, and he thanked him.
Hamza dropped the glass on the tile, and it cracked.
Bilal thanked his teachers, who had helped him.
questions.e: A pronoun must have one clear antecedent. In the last sentence 'who' can only mean the teachers and 'him' can only mean Bilal. In the others 'she' could be Ayesha or her sister, 'he' and 'him' could be either the teacher or Usman, and 'it' could be the glass or the tile.

questions.s: Identify the error: Since the new manager (A) took over, sales (B) are rising (C) steadily and complaints (D) have fallen.
questions.e: When a 'since' clause gives the starting point of a change that continues to now, the main verb takes a perfect tense: 'sales have been rising' (or 'have risen'). 'Took over' is correctly simple past inside the 'since' clause, and 'have fallen' already follows the rule.

questions.s: Choose the correct sentence.
o: When he will come, I will give him the book.
She will phone you after she will finish work.
We will start as soon as the guests will arrive.
I will wait here until you return.
questions.e: In time clauses introduced by when, after, as soon as and until, the simple present is used for the future: 'until you return'. The other three wrongly put 'will' inside the time clause; they should read 'When he comes', 'after she finishes' and 'as soon as the guests arrive'.

questions.s: My little brother is very fond ______ reading comics.
questions.e: The adjective 'fond' is always followed by 'of': 'fond of reading'. Learners often write 'fond with' or 'fond about' by analogy with 'pleased with' or 'excited about', but those prepositions do not go with 'fond'.

questions.s: Choose the correct sentence.
o: We will meet in Sunday morning.
questions.e: Prepositions of time: 'on' for days and dates (on Monday, on Sunday morning), 'in' for months, years and parts of the day (in March), 'at' for clock times (at 9 o'clock). So only 'The exam is on Monday' is correct; the others need 'on Sunday morning', 'in March' and 'at 9 o'clock'.

questions.s: Identify the error: We (A) discussed (B) about the problem (C) for an hour but (D) reached no decision.
questions.e: 'Discuss' is a transitive verb and takes a direct object with no preposition: 'We discussed the problem'. 'About' is used with the noun ('a discussion about') but not with the verb. 'For an hour' and 'reached no decision' are correct.

questions.s: This mobile phone is superior ______ that one.
questions.e: Latin comparatives such as superior, inferior, senior, junior, prior and preferable are followed by 'to', not 'than': 'superior to that one'. 'Than' is tempting because 'superior' means 'better', but it is used only with -er and 'more' comparatives.

questions.s: He was accused ______ stealing the documents.
questions.e: The verb 'accuse' takes 'of': 'accused of stealing'. 'With' goes with 'charge' ('charged with theft'), and 'for' is used with 'blame' or 'punish' ('punished for stealing'), which is why they are easy to confuse.

questions.s: Choose the correct sentence.
o: Our team consists of ten girls.
He entered into the room quietly.
We reached to Lahore at noon.
questions.e: 'Consist' is followed by 'of': 'consists of ten girls'. 'Prefer' takes 'to' (prefers tea to coffee), and 'enter' (a room) and 'reach' (a place) take a direct object with no preposition: 'entered the room', 'reached Lahore'.

questions.s: Identify the error: Bilal (A) is married (B) with a doctor (C) who works (D) at a hospital in Rawalpindi.
questions.e: The adjective 'married' is followed by 'to', not 'with': 'Bilal is married to a doctor'. 'Who works' is the correct relative pronoun for a person with a singular verb, and 'at a hospital' is correct.

questions.s: My grandmother is afraid ______ dogs.
questions.e: The adjective 'afraid' is followed by 'of': 'afraid of dogs'. 'Afraid from' is a common error made by translating directly from Urdu ('se darna'), but English uses 'of' here.

questions.s: Choose the correct sentence.
o: It all depends of the weather.
She was absent in the class yesterday.
We should comply with the rules.
She is not familiar about this area.
questions.e: 'Comply' is followed by 'with': 'comply with the rules'. The others need 'depends on', 'absent from (the) class' and 'familiar with this area'; each wrong sentence uses a preposition that does not go with that verb or adjective.

questions.s: He has been charged ______ murder.
questions.e: In the legal sense, a person is 'charged with' a crime: 'charged with murder'. 'Of' goes with 'accused' (accused of murder) and 'guilty' (guilty of murder), which is why it is tempting. 'Charged for' refers to paying money for something.

questions.s: Identify the error: (A) Despite of the heavy rain, (B) the match continued, and the crowd (C) stayed (D) until the end.
questions.e: 'Despite' is a preposition on its own and is never followed by 'of': 'Despite the heavy rain'. The phrase 'in spite of' does take 'of', and mixing the two produces 'despite of'. 'Until the end' is correct.

questions.s: I am looking forward ______ you next month.
questions.e: In 'look forward to', 'to' is a preposition, so it is followed by a noun or an -ing form, not the base verb: 'looking forward to seeing you'. 'To see' is the most tempting choice because 'to' is usually part of an infinitive.

questions.s: The doctor advised him to abstain ______ sugary drinks.
questions.e: The verb 'abstain' is followed by 'from', like 'refrain from' and 'keep away from': 'abstain from sugary drinks'. 'Off' is used in the informal phrasal verb 'keep off', and 'against' goes with 'advise against', which is why they may seem possible.

questions.s: Identify the error: Although we (A) offered, Sana (B) insisted to pay (C) for (D) the whole meal.
questions.e: 'Insist' is followed by 'on' + -ing, not by a to-infinitive: 'Sana insisted on paying'. 'Pay for' (the meal) is correct. Learners confuse 'insist' with verbs such as 'want' and 'decide', which do take 'to'.

questions.s: Choose the correct sentence.
o: She came to college by foot.
He arrived to Lahore at night.
We went to Islamabad by train.
They travelled in bus to Multan.
questions.e: Means of transport take 'by' with no article: 'by train', 'by bus', 'by car'. The exception is walking, which is 'on foot', not 'by foot'. 'Arrive' takes 'in' for a city or country ('arrived in Lahore'), never 'to'.

questions.s: Choose the correct sentence.
o: He is senior than me in the office.
She is responsible of the accounts.
I am capable to solve this problem.
questions.e: 'Interested' is followed by 'in'. The others need 'senior to' (Latin comparatives take 'to'), 'responsible for' and 'capable of solving'; 'capable' is never followed by a to-infinitive.

questions.s: The novel was translated ______ Urdu last year.
questions.e: A text is translated 'into' another language, because the preposition shows change from one form to another, as in 'convert into' and 'change into'. 'Onto' shows movement to a surface, and 'at' and 'with' do not combine with 'translate' in this sense.

questions.s: She has been suffering ______ fever since Tuesday.
questions.e: The verb 'suffer' takes 'from' before an illness or problem: 'suffering from fever'. 'Suffering of' is a common error, perhaps by analogy with 'die of', but 'suffer' does not take 'of'.

questions.s: Identify the error: The new rule (A) prevents students (B) to use (C) their phones (D) during lectures.
questions.e: 'Prevent' follows the pattern 'prevent somebody from doing something': 'prevents students from using their phones'. A to-infinitive cannot follow 'prevent'. 'Prevents' agrees with the singular 'rule', and 'during lectures' is correct.

questions.s: Identify the error: Zainab's parents (A) were (B) delighted, and (C) she was proud (D) for her brother's success.
questions.e: The adjective 'proud' is followed by 'of': 'proud of her brother's success'. 'Were' agrees with the plural 'parents', and 'she was proud' is correct. 'For' is used with 'happy for' someone, which is why it slips in here.

questions.s: Ali was born ______ 2008.
questions.e: Years, months and seasons take 'in': 'born in 2008', 'in March', 'in winter'. 'On' is for days and full dates (born on 5 May 2008), and 'at' is for clock times, so neither fits a year on its own.

questions.s: It took us ______ hour to reach Murree.
questions.e: The choice between 'a' and 'an' depends on the first sound, not the first letter. In 'hour' the h is silent and the word begins with a vowel sound, so it takes 'an': 'an hour'. 'A hour' follows the spelling rather than the sound.

questions.s: Identify the error: He (A) hopes to (B) join (C) an university (D) abroad.
questions.e: 'University' begins with a 'you' sound, which is a consonant sound, so it takes 'a': 'a university', like 'a uniform' and 'a European'. 'An' is used only before a vowel sound. 'Hopes to join' and 'abroad' are correct.

questions.s: ______ Indus is the longest river in Pakistan.
questions.e: Names of rivers, seas, oceans and deserts take the definite article: 'the Indus', 'the Arabian Sea', 'the Thar'. The superlative 'the longest' also shows that one particular thing is meant, so 'a' and 'an' are wrong.

questions.s: Identify the error: (A) The Mount Everest is (B) the highest (C) peak in (D) the world.
questions.e: Names of single mountains take no article: 'Mount Everest', 'K2', 'Nanga Parbat'. Mountain ranges do take 'the' (the Himalayas, the Karakoram). 'The highest' (superlative) and 'the world' (unique thing) correctly use 'the'.

questions.s: Choose the correct sentence.
o: He gave me many advices before the exam.
He bought a new furniture for his room.
Can you give me some information?
I need a informations about the hostel.
questions.e: Advice, furniture and information are uncountable nouns: they have no plural and do not take 'a' or 'an'. 'Some information' is correct. To count them, use 'a piece of advice' or 'an item of furniture'.

questions.s: Choose the correct sentence.
o: He gave me an useful tip.
questions.e: 'One' begins with a 'w' sound, a consonant sound, so 'a one-eyed cat' is correct. 'European' and 'useful' begin with a 'you' sound and take 'a', while 'honest' begins with a vowel sound (silent h) and takes 'an'. The rule depends on sound, not spelling.

questions.s: Identify the error: The technician (A) took (B) a X-ray (C) of my (D) wrist.
questions.e: The letter X is pronounced 'eks', which begins with a vowel sound, so it takes 'an': 'an X-ray', like 'an MBA' and 'an FIR'. The article follows the sound of the first letter, not whether it is written as a consonant.

questions.s: Identify the error: Sana (A) is (B) tallest girl (C) in (D) our class.
questions.e: A superlative adjective before a noun takes the definite article, because it picks out one particular person: 'the tallest girl in our class'. 'In our class' is the correct preposition after a superlative, and 'is' agrees with 'Sana'.

questions.s: ______ Himalayas stretch across several countries.
questions.e: Mountain ranges, like groups of islands, take 'the': 'the Himalayas', 'the Karakoram', 'the Alps'. 'A' and 'an' cannot go with a plural noun, and 'some' cannot come before a proper name.

questions.s: He was ______ honest man that everyone trusted him.
questions.e: Before an adjective + singular countable noun, use 'such a/an', with the article chosen by sound: 'honest' has a silent h, so 'such an honest man'. 'So' is used before an adjective alone ('so honest that'), and 'such a' ignores the vowel sound.

questions.s: Choose the correct sentence.
o: The nature is at its best in spring.
The United States has fifty states.
She is a doctor and her husband is engineer.
She is learning the English at an institute.
questions.e: Country names that contain words like 'States', 'Kingdom' or 'Republic' take 'the', and the name is treated as one country with a singular verb. 'Nature' in the general sense and names of languages ('English') take no article, and a singular job noun needs 'a' or 'an': 'an engineer'.

questions.s: Identify the error: We (A) are having (B) such (C) a lovely weather (D) in Murree this week.
questions.e: 'Weather' is an uncountable noun, so it cannot take 'a' or 'an', even after 'such' or 'what': 'such lovely weather'. 'Are having' is correct, since 'have' here means 'experience' and can be continuous. 'In Murree' is the right preposition for a town.

questions.s: Choose the correct sentence.
o: The honesty is the best policy.
She plays the cricket every evening.
He went to the bed early last night.
We had dinner at a small café.
questions.e: Meals in general take no article ('had dinner'), and 'a small café' is a singular countable noun mentioned for the first time. Abstract nouns used in a general sense (honesty), names of sports (cricket) and the fixed phrase 'go to bed' take no article.

questions.s: Hamza was ______ first person to reach the summit.
questions.e: Ordinal numbers such as first, second and last pick out one particular person or thing, so they take the definite article: 'the first person'. 'A first person' and 'one first person' are not used in this sense.

questions.s: Identify the error: Last night (A) the stars were hidden, but (B) moon (C) was (D) unusually bright.
questions.e: Things that are unique in our world, such as the sun, the moon and the sky, take the definite article: 'but the moon was unusually bright'. 'The stars were' correctly uses a plural verb, and 'unusually' is the adverb modifying 'bright'.

questions.s: Identify the error: (A) The Karakoram Highway links Pakistan (B) with (C) the China (D) through the Khunjerab Pass.
questions.e: Most country names take no article: 'Pakistan', 'China', 'Iran'. Only names with words such as 'States', 'Kingdom' or 'Republic', or plural names, take 'the'. Named highways and passes, such as 'the Karakoram Highway' and 'the Khunjerab Pass', do take 'the'.

questions.s: Choose the correct sentence.
o: The cattle is grazing in the field.
There is many reasons for his success.
Measles is a highly infectious disease.
questions.e: Names of diseases ending in -s, such as measles and mumps, are singular: 'Measles is'. 'Cattle' is always plural ('are grazing'), 'trousers' is a plural-only noun ('need ironing'), and after 'there' the verb agrees with 'many reasons' ('There are').

questions.s: Identify the error: The results (A) of the survey (B) shows that most (C) students (D) prefer online classes.
questions.e: The subject is the plural 'The results'; 'of the survey' only describes it. So the verb must be plural: 'The results ... show'. The singular 'survey' just before the verb makes 'shows' look right. 'Most students prefer' correctly agrees.

questions.s: Either Ali or his sisters ______ going to pick you up.
questions.e: With 'either ... or', the verb agrees with the subject nearer to it. 'His sisters' is plural and next to the verb, so 'are going'. 'Is' would be correct only if the order were reversed: 'Either his sisters or Ali is going'.

questions.s: Identify the error: Neither (A) the players nor (B) the coach (C) were happy (D) with the referee's decision.
questions.e: With 'neither ... nor', the verb agrees with the nearer subject. Here 'the coach' is singular and nearer, so the verb should be 'was happy'. The plural 'players' at the start makes 'were' seem right. 'Happy with' a decision is the correct preposition.

questions.s: Choose the correct sentence.
o: One of my friends live in Canada.
Each of the rooms have a fan.
The list of names are on the notice board.
questions.e: Indefinite pronouns such as everybody, everyone and nobody take a singular verb: 'Everybody likes'. 'One of ...', 'Each of ...' and 'The list of ...' also have singular subjects (one, each, list), so they need 'lives', 'has' and 'is'.

questions.s: ______ turn is it to read the next paragraph?
questions.e: 'Whose' is the possessive question word, used before a noun: 'Whose turn is it?' 'Who's' is the short form of 'who is' or 'who has', so it cannot come before 'turn'; 'who' and 'whom' cannot show possession.

questions.s: Identify the error: Please (A) send (B) the final report (C) to Bilal or (D) myself by Friday.
questions.e: A reflexive pronoun such as 'myself' is used only when it refers back to the subject of the same clause (I hurt myself) or for emphasis. Here the subject is the understood 'you', so the object form is needed: 'to Bilal or me'. Using 'myself' to sound polite is a common error.

questions.s: ______ and I have known each other since school.
questions.e: Pronouns that form part of the subject take the subject case: 'She and I have known'. Drop 'and I' to test it: 'She has known', not 'Her has known'. 'Hers' is a possessive and 'Herself' a reflexive, and neither can be a subject.

questions.s: Identify the error: (A) Us engineers (B) must (C) always check (D) our calculations twice.
questions.e: When a pronoun comes before a noun in the subject, it takes the subject case: 'We engineers must'. Test by removing the noun: 'We must check', not 'Us must check'. 'Our calculations' is the correct possessive.

questions.s: Choose the correct sentence.
o: The boy which won the race is my cousin.
This is the house that my grandfather built.
The teacher whom gave us the test was strict.
Is this the pen who you lost?
questions.e: 'That' can be used as a relative pronoun for things (and people), so 'the house that my grandfather built' is correct. 'Which' is for things, not people ('The boy who won'), 'who' is for people, not things ('the pen that/which you lost'), and 'whom' cannot be the subject of 'gave'.

questions.s: The principal invited Fatima and ______ to the ceremony.
questions.e: The pronoun is part of the object of 'invited', so it takes the object case: 'invited Fatima and me'. Drop 'Fatima and' to test it: 'invited me', not 'invited I'. 'Myself' is reflexive and needs 'I' as the subject of the clause.

questions.s: Choose the correct sentence.
o: The number of girls has doubled.
Every one of the books were damaged in the flood.
The children has gone to bed early.
She come home late every night.
questions.e: 'The number of' + plural noun takes a singular verb, because the subject is 'number': 'The number of girls has doubled'. 'Every one of' is also singular ('was damaged'), 'children' is plural ('have gone'), and 'She' needs 'comes'.

questions.s: Identify the error: The children (A) were playing (B) cricket when (C) it starts (D) to rain.
questions.e: The tenses in a past narrative must be consistent. A past action in progress (were playing) interrupted by a short action takes the simple past for the interruption: 'when it started to rain'. 'Starts' wrongly switches to the present.

questions.s: She is jealous ______ her sister's success.
questions.e: The adjective 'jealous' is followed by 'of', like 'envious of' and 'proud of': 'jealous of her sister's success'. 'From' is a direct translation from Urdu ('se jalna') and is not used with 'jealous' in English.

questions.s: Identify the error: Usman (A) has (B) a good (C) command (D) on English.
questions.e: In the sense of knowing a language or skill well, 'command' is followed by 'of': 'a good command of English'. 'A good command' correctly uses 'a' with this countable use of the noun. 'On' is a common error by analogy with 'hold on' or 'control over'.

questions.s: She has been working on the project ______ the past three months.
questions.e: 'The past three months' is a length of time, so it takes 'for' with the present perfect continuous. 'Since' is used only with a starting point ('since May'). 'From' needs a matching 'to' or 'until' and cannot introduce a period like this.

questions.s: Choose the correct sentence.
o: He is studying the medicine in Karachi.
He travels to work by the bus.
I have lived here for a decade.
questions.e: 'A decade' is a singular countable noun naming a length of time, so 'for a decade' is correct. Academic subjects in general take no article ('studying medicine'), 'by + transport' takes no article ('by bus'), and 'umbrella' begins with a vowel sound, so 'an umbrella'.

questions.s: Identify the error: The rich (A) is not always (B) happy, and the poor (C) are not always (D) miserable.
questions.e: 'The + adjective' used for a group of people (the rich, the poor, the young) is plural and takes a plural verb: 'The rich are not always happy'. The sentence itself shows the right form in 'the poor are'. 'Happy' and 'miserable' are adjectives after the verb 'be'.

questions.s: Choose the correct sentence.
o: Sana has went to Skardu twice.
Sana is visiting Skardu twice so far.
Sana had visited Skardu twice so far.
Sana has been to Skardu twice so far.
questions.e: Experiences up to now, with 'so far', 'ever' or a number of times, take the present perfect: 'has been to Skardu twice'. 'Has went' uses the past tense instead of the past participle 'gone', and 'had visited' (past perfect) does not fit 'so far', which means 'up to now'.

questions.s: Identify the error: Scarcely (A) had the guests (B) sat down (C) than the (D) food arrived.
questions.e: 'Scarcely' and 'hardly' are followed by 'when' (or 'before'), not 'than': 'Scarcely had the guests sat down when the food arrived'. 'Than' belongs only with 'no sooner'. 'Had the guests sat' correctly inverts the subject and auxiliary after a negative adverb.

questions.s: Identify the error in the sentence: Five hundred rupees (A) are (B) too much (C) to pay (D) for this pen.
questions.e: A plural amount of money, time or distance treated as one sum takes a singular verb: 'Five hundred rupees is too much.' The phrase 'too much' shows the amount is thought of as a single quantity. The other marked parts are correct.

questions.s: Choose the correct sentence.
o: Not only the students but also the teacher were late.
Not only the students but also the teacher was late.
Not only the students but also the teacher are late.
Not only the students but the teacher also were late.
questions.e: With 'not only ... but also', the verb agrees with the subject nearer to it. The nearer subject is 'the teacher' (singular), so the verb is 'was'. The plural 'students' comes first and makes 'were' look right, but it does not control the verb.

questions.s: Choose the best replacement for the part in capitals: The scissors IS on the top shelf.
questions.e: Nouns for things made of two joined parts, such as scissors, trousers and spectacles, have no singular form and always take a plural verb: 'The scissors are on the top shelf.' (With 'a pair of scissors' the verb is singular, because 'pair' is the subject.)

questions.s: Identify the error in the sentence: All the (A) furniture in these (B) rooms (C) are (D) new.
questions.e: 'Furniture' is an uncountable noun, so it is singular and takes 'is': 'All the furniture in these rooms is new.' The plural 'rooms' is inside a phrase describing the furniture and does not decide the verb.

questions.s: Choose the correct sentence.
o: The rest of the guests has gone home.
The rest of the guest have gone home.
The rest of guests has gone home.
The rest of the guests have gone home.
questions.e: With 'the rest of', the verb agrees with the noun after 'of'. 'The rest of the guests' means the other guests, a plural group, so the verb is 'have'. (With an uncountable noun it is singular: 'The rest of the cake is in the fridge.')

questions.s: Choose the best replacement for the part in capitals: THESE KIND OF QUESTIONS ARE easy to solve.
questions.e: 'Kind' is singular, so it takes the singular 'this' and a singular verb: 'This kind of question is easy.' 'These kind' pairs a plural determiner with a singular noun, which is a common error.

questions.s: Choose the best replacement for the part in capitals: We HAVE BEEN WAITING for an hour when the bus finally arrived.
questions.e: An action that continued up to a point in the past takes the past perfect continuous: 'We had been waiting for an hour when the bus arrived.' 'Have been waiting' measures time up to now, which clashes with the past 'arrived'.

questions.s: Identify the error in the sentence: When I (A) was a child, I (B) used to (C) walking (D) to school.
questions.e: 'Used to' for a past habit is followed by the base form of the verb: 'I used to walk to school.' The -ing form follows 'be used to', which has a different meaning (be accustomed to).

questions.s: Choose the correct sentence.
o: Sana is used to get up early.
Sana used to getting up early.
Sana is used to getting up early.
Sana is use to getting up early.
questions.e: 'Be used to' means 'be accustomed to'. Here 'to' is a preposition, so it is followed by the -ing form: 'is used to getting up'. 'Is used to get up' wrongly uses the base verb, and 'used to getting' drops the verb 'is'.

questions.s: Choose the best replacement for the part in capitals: I failed the test. I wish I HAVE STUDIED harder.
questions.e: A wish about the past (a regret) takes the past perfect: 'I wish I had studied harder.' 'I wish I studied' would be a wish about the present, and 'have studied' or 'would study' cannot express regret about a finished past event.

questions.s: Choose the correct sentence.
o: Have you ever been to Gwadar?
Did you ever went to Gwadar?
Have you ever went to Gwadar?
Are you ever been to Gwadar?
questions.e: Questions about life experience with 'ever' use the present perfect: have + past participle. The participle used here is 'been'. 'Went' is the past simple and cannot follow 'did' or 'have', and 'are ... been' is not a tense.

questions.s: Choose the best replacement for the part in capitals: Listen! Someone KNOCKS at the door.
questions.e: An action happening at the moment of speaking takes the present continuous: 'Someone is knocking at the door.' 'Listen!' shows the knocking is going on now. The present simple 'knocks' is for habits and general facts.

questions.s: Identify the error in the sentence: Let (A) him and (B) I (C) carry (D) the boxes.
questions.e: 'Let' is followed by object pronouns, so both pronouns must be in the object form: 'Let him and me carry the boxes.' 'I' is a subject pronoun. 'Him' is already correct, and 'carry' is the base form needed after 'let'.

questions.s: Choose the correct sentence.
o: The man who I thought was the manager turned out to be a visitor.
The man whom I thought was the manager turned out to be a visitor.
The man which I thought was the manager turned out to be a visitor.
The man whose I thought was the manager turned out to be a visitor.
questions.e: The relative pronoun is the subject of 'was the manager'; 'I thought' is only an inserted clause. A subject takes 'who', not the object form 'whom'. Test it by removing 'I thought': 'the man who was the manager'. 'Which' is not used for people, and 'whose' shows possession.

questions.s: Identify the error in the sentence: This (A) car is not (B) ours; (C) it is (D) their's.
questions.e: Possessive pronouns (yours, ours, theirs, hers, its) never take an apostrophe, so the correct form is 'theirs'. 'Ours' in the same sentence is already written correctly.

questions.s: Identify the error in the sentence: The boy (A) which (B) won the race (C) is (D) my cousin.
questions.e: The relative pronoun 'who' (or 'that') is used for people, and 'which' for things and animals. The boy is a person, so the sentence should read 'The boy who won the race is my cousin'.

questions.s: Choose the correct sentence.
o: Hamza hurt hisself while playing cricket.
Hamza hurt himselves while playing cricket.
Hamza hurt himself while playing cricket.
Hamza hurt herself while playing cricket.
questions.e: The reflexive pronoun for 'he' is 'himself', used when the object is the same person as the subject. 'Hisself' is not standard English, 'himselves' does not exist, and 'herself' does not agree with Hamza.

questions.s: Identify the error in the sentence: The train (A) arrived (B) to (C) the station (D) on time.
questions.e: 'Arrive' takes 'at' for a building or point such as a station or airport, and 'in' for a city or country. It never takes 'to': 'The train arrived at the station on time.' 'On time' is correct.

questions.s: Choose the best replacement for the part in capitals: Our picnic DEPENDS FROM the weather.
questions.e: The verb 'depend' takes the preposition 'on' (or 'upon'): 'Our picnic depends on the weather.' 'From' and 'of' are common mistakes, and 'depend' is not normally used in the continuous form with this meaning.

questions.s: Choose the correct sentence.
o: Ali listens at music every evening.
Ali listens with music every evening.
Ali listens to music every evening.
questions.e: 'Listen' needs the preposition 'to' before its object: 'listens to music'. Unlike 'hear', it cannot take an object directly, so 'listens music' is wrong; 'at' and 'with' are not used with 'listen' in this sense.

questions.s: Identify the error in the sentence: Hamza (A) is (B) capable (C) to solve (D) difficult problems.
questions.e: The adjective 'capable' takes the preposition 'of' followed by the -ing form: 'capable of solving difficult problems'. 'Able' takes a to-infinitive ('able to solve'), which is why 'capable to' is a common mix-up.

questions.s: Choose the best replacement for the part in capitals: The students ENTERED INTO the hall quietly.
