questions.e: When it means going into a place, 'enter' takes its object directly: 'The students entered the hall.' 'Enter into' is used for things such as an agreement or a discussion, not a room. 'In' and 'inside' are also unnecessary after 'enter'.

questions.s: Choose the best replacement for the part in capitals: Your answer is SIMILAR WITH mine.
questions.e: The adjective 'similar' is followed by the preposition 'to': 'Your answer is similar to mine.' 'With', 'from' and 'as' are not used after 'similar'; 'mine' correctly stands for 'my answer'.

questions.s: Choose the best replacement for the part in capitals: I prefer tea THAN coffee.
questions.e: 'Prefer' compares two things with 'to', not 'than': 'I prefer tea to coffee.' 'Prefer' is not a comparative adjective, so 'than' cannot follow it. 'Over than' joins two prepositions, and 'from' is not used with 'prefer'.

questions.s: Identify the error in the sentence: She (A) met (B) an European (C) tourist (D) in Lahore.
questions.e: The article depends on the first sound. 'European' begins with a 'yoo' sound, which is a consonant sound, so it takes 'a': 'a European tourist'. The written vowel 'E' makes 'an' look right, but the sound decides.

questions.s: Choose the correct sentence.
o: The honesty is the best policy.
An honesty is the best policy.
questions.e: Abstract nouns such as honesty, courage and patience take no article when used in a general sense: 'Honesty is the best policy.' A superlative such as 'best' takes 'the', so 'a best policy' is wrong.

questions.s: Choose the best replacement for the part in capitals: Zainab wants to become DOCTOR.
questions.e: A singular countable noun naming a profession needs an article: 'Zainab wants to become a doctor.' 'Doctor' begins with a consonant sound, so it takes 'a', not 'an'. 'The doctors' is plural and does not fit one person.

questions.s: Choose the best replacement for the part in capitals: Luckily, I still had FEW RUPEES left, so I could buy a cup of tea.
questions.e: 'A few' means 'some, a small number', which is positive, while 'few' means 'hardly any', which is negative. 'Luckily' and 'so I could buy' show a positive meaning, so 'a few rupees' is right. 'Little' and 'a little' are used with uncountable nouns, not with 'rupees'.

questions.s: Choose the best replacement for the part in capitals: I have A GOOD NEWS for you.
questions.e: 'News' is an uncountable noun: it has no plural and does not take 'a' or 'an'. So the correct form is 'I have good news for you' (or 'a piece of good news'). 'Newses' does not exist.

questions.s: Choose the correct sentence.
o: Looking out of the window, the mountains seemed covered in snow.
Looking out of the window, Sana saw snow on the mountains.
Looking out of the window, the snow lay on the mountains.
Looking out of the window, there was snow on the mountains.
questions.e: An opening participle phrase describes the subject that follows it. Only Sana can look out of the window, so she must be the subject: 'Sana saw snow on the mountains'. With 'the mountains' or 'the snow' as subject the modifier dangles, and 'there was' gives it no subject at all.

questions.s: Choose the correct sentence.
o: The man was walking a dog in a blue jacket.
The man in a blue jacket was walking a dog.
In a blue jacket, a dog was walked by the man.
The man was walking in a blue jacket a dog.
questions.e: The phrase 'in a blue jacket' describes the man, so it should come straight after 'The man'. Placed after 'a dog', it suggests the dog wore the jacket: a misplaced modifier. At the start of a passive sentence it describes the dog again.

questions.s: Identify the error in the sentence: The course teaches students (A) how to think, (B) how to write and (C) speaking (D) in public.
questions.e: The list after 'teaches students' must be parallel. The first two items are 'how to think' and 'how to write', so the third must be 'how to speak', not the gerund 'speaking'.

questions.s: Choose the correct sentence.
o: You can either stay here or you can come with us.
You can either stay here or come with us.
Either you can stay here or come with us.
You can stay either here or come with us.
questions.e: 'Either' and 'or' must be followed by the same kind of element. In 'either stay here or come with us' both are followed by a verb phrase. The other sentences pair a verb with a clause, a clause with a verb, or an adverb with a verb.

questions.s: Identify the error in the sentence: Shahid is (A) one of the (B) best (C) player (D) in the team.
questions.e: 'One of the' + superlative is followed by a plural noun, because a person is picked out from a group: 'one of the best players'. The superlative 'best' is correct because Shahid is compared with the whole team.

questions.s: Choose the correct sentence.
o: If it will be sunny tomorrow, we will go to the zoo.
If it is sunny tomorrow, we would go to the zoo.
If it was sunny tomorrow, we will go to the zoo.
If it is sunny tomorrow, we will go to the zoo.
questions.e: A real future possibility takes the first conditional: present simple in the if-clause and 'will' in the main clause. 'Will' does not go in the if-clause, and 'is ... would' or 'was ... will' mix two conditional types.

questions.s: Choose the correct passive form of: Someone has stolen my bicycle.
questions.e: The present perfect passive is has/have + been + past participle: 'has been stolen'. The agent 'someone' is unknown, so it is left out. 'Has stolen' is active, and the participle of 'steal' is 'stolen', not 'stole'.

questions.s: Choose the correct indirect form of: Hamza said to me, "Have you seen my keys?"
o: Hamza asked me if had I seen his keys.
Hamza asked me if I have seen my keys.
Hamza said to me that had I seen his keys.
Hamza asked me if I had seen his keys.
questions.e: A yes/no question is reported with 'asked' + 'if/whether' and statement order. The present perfect moves back to the past perfect (have seen → had seen), 'you' becomes 'I' and 'my' becomes 'his'. 'If had I seen' keeps question order, and 'my keys' keeps the wrong pronoun.

questions.s: Identify the error in the sentence: Hamza (A) is two years (B) elder (C) than (D) his cousin.
questions.e: 'Elder' is used for family members, mostly before a noun ('my elder brother'), and is never followed by 'than'. In a comparison with 'than', the form is 'older': 'Hamza is two years older than his cousin.'

questions.s: Choose the correct passive form of: They will announce the results tomorrow.
o: The results will been announced tomorrow.
The results will be announced tomorrow.
The results would be announced tomorrow.
questions.e: The future simple passive is will + be + past participle: 'The results will be announced tomorrow.' 'Will announce' is active and says the results do the announcing, 'will been' leaves out 'be', and 'would' changes the tense.

questions.s: Choose the correct indirect form of: Ali said, "Let us go for a walk."
o: Ali suggested to go for a walk.
Ali suggested them to go for a walk.
Ali suggested that they should go for a walk.
Ali said that let us go for a walk.
questions.e: A suggestion beginning 'Let us' is reported with 'suggested' (or 'proposed') + that-clause with 'should': 'Ali suggested that they should go for a walk.' 'Suggest' is not followed by a to-infinitive or by 'them to', and 'let us' cannot be kept inside a that-clause.

questions.s: According to the passage, the nitrogen and oxygen molecules that scatter sunlight are
o: much larger than the wavelength of visible light
about the same size as the droplets in clouds
far smaller than the wavelength of visible light
made mostly of water vapour from the oceans
questions.e: The third sentence says the molecules are far smaller than the wavelength of visible light. Cloud droplets are described later as ‘larger particles’ that scatter all colours equally, so the molecules are not the same size as them.

questions.s: Based on the passage, an observer on the Moon, which has almost no atmosphere, would most likely see a daytime sky that is
questions.e: The passage explains that the sky looks blue because air molecules scatter sunlight towards our eyes from every direction. With almost no atmosphere there is almost nothing to scatter light, so the sky away from the Sun would look black. Blue is tempting only if one forgets that the colour comes from the air, not from sunlight itself.

questions.s: The question ‘why is the sky not violet?’ is raised mainly in order to
o: show that Lord Rayleigh's mathematics was mistaken
suggest that the sky is in fact slightly violet
explain why clouds appear white rather than blue
address a puzzle the explanation seems to raise
questions.e: Since the passage has just said that violet is scattered even more than blue, a reader might expect a violet sky; the next sentence gives three reasons why it is not. Nothing in the passage says Rayleigh's mathematics was wrong, and clouds are explained separately at the end.

questions.s: The passage is mainly concerned with
o: the work of two French surveyors in the eighteenth century
how a shared system of measurement arose and spread
the reasons why traders resisted all new units
the methods used to measure the speed of light
questions.e: The passage moves from the confusion of local units to the French design of the metre, litre and kilogram, then to its slow acceptance and worldwide spread. The surveyors are one detail in that story, and the speed of light appears only in the final sentence.

questions.s: In the passage, the word ‘refined’ most nearly means
questions.e: The sentence explains that the metre is now fixed by the speed of light, which can be measured ‘far more precisely’ than the Earth, so the definitions have been made more exact. ‘Purified’ is a meaning of refined used for sugar or oil, not for definitions.

questions.s: According to the passage, the metre is now defined using the speed of light because
o: it can be measured more accurately than the Earth
the size of the Earth had changed since the 1790s
the original survey was found to have no errors
people in France still preferred their familiar old units
questions.e: The last sentence says the speed of light can be measured far more precisely than the size of the Earth. The passage never claims that the Earth itself changed, and French attachment to old units explains the system's slow start, not its later redefinition.

questions.s: According to the passage, ice floats on water because
o: ice is less dense than liquid water
ice contains trapped bubbles of air
cold water always rises to the top
ice molecules are heavier than water
questions.e: The passage says water expands by about nine per cent when it freezes, so ‘Ice is therefore less dense than liquid water, and it floats.’ The empty space in ice comes from the open pattern of hydrogen bonds, not from trapped air bubbles.

questions.s: As used in the passage, the word ‘open’ in ‘a fixed, open pattern’ most nearly means
questions.e: The phrase is explained at once: the pattern ‘contains a great deal of empty space’, so open means full of gaps. ‘Honest and frank’ is the sense used for people, not for the arrangement of molecules.

questions.s: It can be inferred that if ice were denser than liquid water, lakes in cold regions would most likely
questions.e: Lakes freeze from the top down only because the floating ice forms a lid. If ice were denser, it would sink as it formed and collect on the bottom, so a lake would fill with ice from below. The passage gives no reason to think the water would stop freezing altogether.

questions.s: According to the passage, Deosai was declared a national park mainly to
o: control the number of golden marmots
build better jeep tracks for visitors
study the plateau's summer wild flowers
questions.e: The passage says the plateau became a national park in 1993 ‘largely to protect the Himalayan brown bear’, whose numbers had fallen very low. Marmots are mentioned as bear food and as noticeable animals, not as the reason for the park.

questions.s: As used in the passage, the word ‘pressures’ most nearly means
questions.e: The sentence about ‘pressures’ is followed by examples of harm from visitors: jeeps damaging soil and litter drawing bears towards people. ‘Physical forces on the ground’ is tempting because of the jeeps, but litter is not a physical force, so the word means strains or burdens in general.

questions.s: It can be inferred that damage to Deosai's soil by vehicles is a particular concern because
o: bears dig up the soil when searching for roots
the flowers there bloom only every few years
the cold climate makes recovery very slow
the soil is too rich to support grassland
questions.e: The passage says the thin soil ‘recovers only slowly in such a cold climate’, so tyre damage lasts a long time. The flowers are said to bloom quickly each short summer, not every few years, and bears eating roots is never linked to soil damage.

questions.s: According to the passage, at a growth rate of 9 per cent a year, an amount doubles in about
questions.e: The passage states that at 9 per cent a sum doubles in about 8 years, which is 72 ÷ 9. Twelve years is the figure given for 6 per cent, and 9 years is the figure for prices rising at 8 per cent.

questions.s: The author mentions that 72 divides neatly by many small whole numbers in order to
o: show that the rule is exact for every rate of growth
prove that interest rates are always whole numbers
suggest that bankers dislike doing mental arithmetic
explain why 72 is a convenient number for the rule
questions.e: The sentence says 72 is chosen partly because it divides neatly by 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 9 and 12, ‘which makes mental arithmetic easy’. The passage calls the rule ‘only an approximation’, so it cannot be showing that the rule is exact.

questions.s: Which of the following can be inferred from the passage?
o: Savings at 4 per cent a year would take about 18 years to double.
The rule of 72 gives exact answers for rates above 15 per cent.
A population growing by 3 per cent a year doubles in 12 years.
Prices rising by 8 per cent a year double roughly every 72 years.
questions.e: Applying the rule as the passage describes, 72 ÷ 4 = 18 years. The passage gives 24 years, not 12, for a population growing at 3 per cent, and it says the rule is reliable only between about 2 and 15 per cent, never exact above that.

questions.s: According to the passage, the refrigerant takes heat from the food when it
o: is pumped out into the kitchen
questions.e: The passage says the refrigerant flows inside the fridge as a cold liquid and, ‘as it turns into vapour’, takes heat from the food. Condensing in the back coils is the step where it gives heat out to the kitchen, the reverse of what the question asks.

questions.s: The example of wet skin feeling cool in a breeze is included in order to
o: show that fridges should stand in breezy rooms
explain why the compressor becomes hot
suggest that people should wet their skin on hot days
questions.e: The example follows the statement that a liquid absorbs heat when it evaporates, the principle on which the fridge works. The compressor's heat is explained later by compression, not by evaporation.

questions.s: Which of the following can be inferred from the passage?
o: The coils at the back of a fridge should be kept fully covered.
A fridge pressed tightly against a wall would likely work less well.
The compressor is the coldest part of the whole refrigerator.
Refrigerant escapes from the closed pipes each time it turns into vapour.
questions.e: The last sentence says a fridge works best with space around its back coils so that heat can escape; pressing it against a wall removes that space. Covering the coils would also trap heat, and the refrigerant moves round a closed loop, so it does not escape.

questions.s: According to the passage, the Greek text on the Rosetta Stone was important because
o: it was the oldest of the three scripts
it named every ruler of ancient Egypt
it was written in a later everyday script
scholars of the time could still read it
questions.e: The passage says the decree appeared in ancient Greek, ‘which scholars could still read’, and so the Greek ‘acted as a key’ to the other two versions. The later everyday script was Demotic, not Greek.

questions.s: According to the passage, earlier attempts to read hieroglyphs failed mainly because scholars
o: had no surviving examples of hieroglyphic writing
could not read any ancient Greek texts
treated every sign as a picture of an idea
refused to look at the Rosetta Stone
questions.e: Champollion showed that the script mixed sound signs with word signs, ‘which is why earlier attempts that treated every sign as a picture had failed’. Hieroglyphs were carved on many temples and tombs, so a lack of examples was not the problem.

questions.s: As used in the passage, the word ‘key’ most nearly means
o: a metal tool for opening locks
a means of solving a problem
a set of notes in music
questions.e: The Greek text ‘acted as a key’ because scholars could read it and use it to work out the meaning of the other two scripts, so it was a means of unlocking a puzzle. The literal metal tool is the everyday sense, which does not fit a written text.

questions.s: According to the passage, about two-thirds of an octopus's nerve cells are found in its
questions.e: The passage states that about two-thirds of the roughly 500 million nerve cells are located in the eight arms ‘rather than in its central brain’. This is why each arm can act with some independence.

questions.s: In the passage, the phrase ‘a master of disguise’ refers to the octopus's ability to
o: escape from tanks through tiny gaps
unscrew the lids of jars for food
questions.e: The sentence that follows the phrase explains it: special skin cells let the octopus change colour and pattern in a fraction of a second to match rocks, sand or seaweed. Escaping through gaps shows flexibility, not disguise.

questions.s: The final sentence suggests that the octopus's abilities are especially remarkable because it
o: must acquire them quickly and mostly alone
learns most of its skills from older octopuses
lives far longer than most other molluscs
uses its central brain to control every arm
questions.e: The last sentence says most octopuses live only one or two years, so what they know must be learned quickly and largely without help from parents. That rules out learning from older octopuses, and the passage says the brain does not need to direct every movement.

questions.s: Based on the passage, a gap of six seconds between a flash and its thunder means the lightning struck about
questions.e: The passage says a three-second gap means about one kilometre, so six seconds means about two kilometres (sound travels about 340 m each second, and 6 × 340 ≈ 2,000 m). ‘Six kilometres’ wrongly treats each second as a kilometre.

questions.s: According to the passage, distant thunder sounds like a long rumble rather than a single crack because
o: light from the flash always reaches the observer well before the sound
the air in the channel is cooler than the surface of the Sun
the lightning channel is only a few centimetres wide
sound from different parts of the channel arrives at different times
questions.e: The passage explains that the channel is several kilometres long, so sound from its different parts arrives at slightly different times and echoes off hills and buildings. The flash arriving first explains the delay before thunder, not its rumbling, and the air is described as hotter, not cooler, than the Sun's surface.

questions.s: The final three sentences of the passage mainly serve to
o: show how the facts described lead to practical safety advice
describe a new and more accurate method of measuring lightning heat
argue that storms are less dangerous than most people believe
explain why lightning never strikes the same place twice
questions.e: The sentence ‘Safety advice follows from these facts’ introduces the advice to go indoors when thunder is first heard, because strikes can occur far from a storm's centre. The passage stresses danger rather than playing it down, so the third option is the reverse of its point.

questions.s: According to the passage, the experiment with a spinning wheel showed that
o: experts are never influenced by anchors
people ignore numbers that they know to be clearly unrelated
shoppers always guess second-hand prices accurately
even a random number could affect people's estimates
questions.e: Tversky and Kahneman found that ‘even a number produced by spinning a wheel’ could influence estimates of unrelated quantities. That is the opposite of people ignoring unrelated numbers, and the passage says experts are ‘not immune’.

questions.s: In the passage, the word ‘immune’ most nearly means
questions.e: ‘Experts are not immune, although knowledge of a subject can reduce the effect’ means experts are still affected by anchors. ‘Protected from disease’ is the medical sense of the word, which does not fit a discussion of judgement.

questions.s: Which of the following situations best illustrates anchoring as described in the passage?
o: Usman buys a particular phone mainly because a close friend recommends it.
Fatima buys a cheaper bag because her budget this month is limited.
Zainab offers more for a car after the seller names a high price first.
Hamza returns a new shirt to the shop after finding it does not fit.
questions.e: Anchoring is an initial number pulling later judgements towards it, as when a seller who opens high ends with a higher agreed price. Zainab's offer is pulled up by the seller's first figure. Usman is swayed by advice, not by a number, so his case is not anchoring.

questions.s: According to the passage, a camel's hump is made up mainly of
questions.e: The passage corrects the common belief directly: ‘In fact, the hump is mostly fat.’ Water is the popular mistake the passage sets out to correct.

questions.s: The passage mentions the camel's breath, kidneys and dung mainly to show how the animal
questions.e: These details follow the sentence ‘The camel's real skill with water lies elsewhere’: concentrated urine, dry dung and moisture recaptured in the nose all save water. None of them is linked to the hump, which the passage says is fat.

questions.s: What can be inferred about the camel's ability to let its body temperature rise during the day?
o: It causes the camel to lose more water through sweating.
It means the hump must be refilled with water each night.
It saves water that would otherwise be lost in sweat.
It makes the camel's blood cells round instead of oval.
questions.e: The passage says that because its temperature can rise, the camel ‘does not need to sweat until it is very hot’, and this is listed among the features that help it survive water loss. So it saves water; the first option states the opposite.

questions.s: According to the passage, the QR code was first designed to
o: track parts used in making cars
questions.e: The passage opens with Denso Wave's workers, who tracked car parts with barcodes that needed several scans per item; the QR code was designed to solve that problem. Payments and menus are later uses that came after phones gained cameras.

questions.s: As used in the passage, the word ‘unwary’ most nearly means
questions.e: The sentence warns that a fake sticker can send a user to a harmful website, and an unwary user is one who does not suspect this trick. ‘Unlucky’ is tempting, but the word describes the user's lack of caution, not chance.

questions.s: According to the passage, the three large corner squares allow a QR code to
o: be used without paying a fee
questions.e: The passage says the corner squares tell a scanner which way up the code is, ‘so it can be read from any angle and at high speed’. Reading a torn or dirty code depends on the extra, repeated information, not on the squares.

questions.s: According to the passage, an uncut onion does not release the irritating gas because
o: it contains no sulfur compounds at all
the gas is produced only when the onion is cooked
the enzyme and sulfur compounds are kept apart
the onion skin traps all of the gas inside
questions.e: The second sentence says the sulfur compounds and the enzyme ‘are kept apart in different parts of its cells’ until a knife breaks the cells. Cooking actually destroys the enzyme, so the gas is not made by cooking.

questions.s: As used in the passage, the word ‘volatile’ most nearly means
o: likely to change suddenly in mood
quick to turn into a vapour
questions.e: Chilling makes the gas ‘less volatile’, meaning it escapes into the air less readily, so less reaches the eyes. The mood sense of volatile describes people, not chemicals.

questions.s: Based on the passage, which of the following would most likely cause the most tears?
o: Slowly cutting a room-temperature onion with a blunt knife
Cutting a chilled onion with a sharp knife beside an open window
Eating a large plate of onions that have been fried
Slicing a boiled onion under a working kitchen fan
questions.e: The passage gives three ways to reduce tears: chilling, a sharp knife and moving air. The first option avoids all three, and a blunt knife crushes more cells. Cooked onions never sting because cooking destroys the enzyme, which rules out the last two options.

questions.s: According to the passage, the time of a pendulum's swing depends mainly on its
questions.e: The passage states that the time of a swing ‘depends on the pendulum's length, not on the weight of the bob’. Width of swing is tempting, but Galileo's observation was that small swings take almost the same time whether wide or narrow.

questions.s: The passage suggests that temperature was a ‘stubborn problem’ for pendulum clocks because
o: cold weather made the gears freeze solid
warm air slowed the swinging bob through extra friction
changes in temperature altered the rod's length
heat made the clock's bob much heavier
questions.e: The passage explains that a metal rod expands in warm weather and contracts in cold, and since timing depends on length, the clock's rate changed. The solution, two metals whose changes in length cancel, confirms that length was the issue, not friction.

questions.s: Based on the passage, a pendulum clock with an uncorrected metal rod would most likely
questions.e: In hot weather the rod expands, and the passage says a longer pendulum swings more slowly, so each swing takes longer and the clock falls behind. ‘Run fast in hot weather’ reverses the link between length and swing time.

questions.s: According to the passage, drops of water reach the storage tank after they
o: are heated by the sun on the poles
run down the mesh into a gutter
are pumped up from the ground
fall as rain onto the hillside
questions.e: The passage says merged drops become heavy enough to run down the mesh into a gutter and then through a pipe to the tank. The nets need no electricity, so no pumping is involved, and almost no rain falls in these places.

questions.s: The beetle of the Namib Desert is mentioned in order to
o: show that fog nets harm desert wildlife
explain why fog forms over the ocean
prove that the nets work without wind
point to a natural model for the idea
questions.e: The passage says the idea ‘was partly inspired by’ the beetle, which collects fog droplets on its back. Nothing suggests harm to wildlife, and the passage states that the nets need steady wind.

questions.s: The author's attitude towards fog harvesting is best described as
o: strongly critical, since the nets rarely collect water
wildly enthusiastic, calling it a cure for all droughts
balanced, noting both its strengths and its limits
indifferent, giving no view on its usefulness
questions.e: The author praises the nets as needing no fuel and being cheap to maintain, but adds that they work only with frequent fog and steady wind and are ‘not a general answer’. That mix of praise and limits is balanced, not wholly critical or enthusiastic.

questions.s: The passage is mainly concerned with
o: the value of the Indus delta mangroves and the conditions they need to survive
the growth of the fishing economy in the villages along the coast south of Karachi
the reasons why Avicennia marina is the only tree able to grow in salt water
a comparison of the carbon stored by coastal forests and by mountain forests
questions.e: The passage first describes the forest, then its benefits (storm protection, fish nurseries, carbon), and finally its need for both fresh and salt water. Fishing is only one of the benefits mentioned, and the passage never claims Avicennia marina is the only salt-tolerant tree; it says this species makes up most of this forest.

questions.s: It can be inferred from the passage that a sharp fall in the amount of river water reaching the delta would most likely
o: make the water around the mangroves less salty
increase the amount of silt settling on the mudflats
reduce the number of mangrove seedlings that survive
have little effect, since mangroves tolerate salt water
questions.e: The passage states: 'When less river water reaches the delta, the water becomes saltier and fewer seedlings survive.' A sharp fall in river water is the extreme case of this. The last option is tempting because mangroves tolerate salt, but the passage stresses that they also need fresh water and silt, and less river water would mean less silt, not more.

questions.s: As used in the passage, the word 'delicate' in 'a delicate balance' most nearly means
questions.e: The sentences that follow show how the balance between fresh and salt water is upset when river flow falls, so 'delicate' here means easily disturbed. 'Finely detailed' and 'gently flavoured' are other senses of delicate (delicate lace, a delicate taste) that do not fit a balance of water.

questions.s: According to the passage, what is the purpose of the vertical shafts along a karez?
o: They lift water to the surface for drinking.
They let sunlight dry out the tunnel walls.
They mark each family's turn to take water.
They gave access for digging and now for cleaning.
questions.e: The passage says the shafts 'were used to remove soil during digging and still allow workers to climb down for cleaning.' Water in a karez flows by gravity to the fields, not up the shafts, and families' turns are 'measured by time', not by the shafts.

questions.s: The author points out that a karez 'can deliver only as much water as seeps into it' mainly in order to
o: show that a karez supplies too little water for farming
explain why a karez seldom exhausts its source of water
suggest that tube wells are a more dependable source
describe the way the tunnels were originally dug
questions.e: The same sentence continues: 'so it rarely drains an aquifer faster than rain and snowmelt refill it.' The limit is presented as a strength that protects the water supply. Nothing in the passage says karez water is too little for farming; the tunnels in fact feed fields and villages.

questions.s: Which of the following can most reasonably be inferred from the passage?
o: A karez can stop flowing without any damage to its tunnel.
Tube wells lose more of their water to evaporation than karezes do.
Karezes failed mainly because families stopped sharing water in turns.
Most of the karezes in Balochistan were dug within recent decades.
questions.e: The end of the passage explains that pumping by tube wells lowers the water table, and 'as the water table sinks below the tunnels, the old channels simply stop flowing.' So a sound tunnel can still run dry. The passage never compares evaporation from tube wells, and it blames falling water tables, not the sharing system, for the decline.

questions.s: Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?
o: The immune system cannot defeat a germ that it has never met before.
Newer vaccines are safer than those made from killed or weakened germs.
Vaccines let the body form memory cells without suffering the disease.
Antibodies destroy germs directly inside the body's white blood cells.
questions.e: The passage explains immune memory and then states that 'a vaccine makes use of this memory without the danger of the disease.' The first option is wrong because the passage says the body does defeat a new germ, only slowly; the passage never compares the safety of different vaccine types.

questions.s: In the passage, the phrase 'presents the immune system with' most nearly means
questions.e: A vaccine 'presents the immune system with a harmless version of the germ', that is, it offers or exposes the immune system to it so the system can respond. 'Awards' suggests a prize given for merit, which does not fit, and 'explains' would require the immune system to be told something in words.

questions.s: According to the passage, newborn babies benefit when most people around them are immune because
o: their mothers' antibodies are made stronger by the community
a germ finds too few hosts to spread far enough to reach them
they receive memory cells from the vaccinated people around them
germs grow weaker each time they pass from one person to another
questions.e: The last sentence says that when most of a community is immune, 'a germ finds too few hosts to spread, and outbreaks fade before they can reach the most vulnerable.' The passage never says memory cells pass from one person to another; each person forms their own.

questions.s: According to the passage, before about 1450 books in Europe were
o: printed with metal type brought from Korea
rare and costly, as each copy took long to make
cheap but often full of copying mistakes
made mostly in the workshops of Mainz
questions.e: The passage says a scribe 'might need months to produce a single copy of a long work, and books were therefore rare and expensive.' Korea is mentioned only to show that movable type existed elsewhere, not as a source of European type.

questions.s: The author mentions printers in China and Korea mainly in order to
o: argue that Gutenberg copied his methods from Asian printers
explain why European books cost more than Asian ones
suggest that the alphabet was first developed in Asia
show that his real achievement was combining the parts
questions.e: Right after noting that 'movable type itself was not new', the author says what made Gutenberg influential was 'the way its parts worked together'. The reference therefore shifts the credit from invention to combination. The passage makes no claim that Gutenberg copied Asian printers, so the first option goes beyond the text.

questions.s: As used in the final sentence, the word 'accumulate' most nearly means
questions.e: Scholars comparing notes and correcting errors made knowledge grow steadily, so 'accumulate' means build up. 'Spread out' is tempting because the passage also says texts 'circulated widely', but accumulation is about growing in amount, not moving outwards.

questions.s: Based on the passage, a waggle run pointing straight down the comb most likely tells other bees to fly
o: to the right of the sun
questions.e: The angle of the run from the vertical equals the angle between the food and the sun, and straight up means 'fly towards the sun'. Straight down is 180° from straight up, so it means the opposite direction, directly away from the sun. Distance is shown by how long the run lasts, not by its direction, so 'a very short distance' does not follow.

questions.s: According to the passage, the length of each waggle run indicates
o: how far away the flowers are
how much nectar the flowers hold
where the sun is in the sky
questions.e: The passage states: 'The length of each waggle run indicates distance: the longer the run lasts, the farther away the flowers are.' The sun's position is linked to the angle of the run, not its length.

questions.s: According to the passage, von Frisch's conclusions were challenged at first because many scientists
o: had watched robotic bees perform other dances
thought the dance signalled scent, not direction
found that bees ignored the position of the sun
doubted that insects could share abstract ideas
questions.e: The passage says his conclusions were challenged 'because many scientists doubted that an insect could communicate abstract information.' The robotic bees came later and supported his view, so they were not a reason for doubt.

questions.s: According to the passage, the opportunity cost of a choice is
o: the total value of every option not chosen
the amount of money spent on the chosen option
the value of the best alternative given up
the difference between a price and a wage
questions.e: The second sentence defines opportunity cost as 'the value of the best alternative you give up when you make a choice.' The Sana example then warns that it is 'not all the other options added together', which rules out the first option.

questions.s: Bilal spends an evening watching a free film instead of helping at his family's bakery, which was his next best choice. According to the ideas in the passage, the opportunity cost of watching the film is
o: the help he could have given at the bakery
nothing at all, because the film was free
the price that a cinema ticket would cost
every other way he could spend the evening
questions.e: Opportunity cost is the best alternative given up, and here that is helping at the bakery. The passage's free concert ticket example shows that a free event still has a cost in time, so 'nothing at all' is wrong; adding up every other option is the mistake the Sana example warns against.

questions.s: In the closing sentences, the author's main point is that opportunity cost
o: shows that the cheapest option is always best
proves that everyone values things alike
applies only to choices involving money
aids comparison but does not decide for us
questions.e: The passage opens with 'The concept does not tell anyone what to choose' and ends by saying it 'encourage[s] a more honest comparison'. It also states that 'people value things differently', which directly contradicts the second option.

questions.s: As used in the passage, the word 'contest' most nearly means
questions.e: The height of the peaks results from two opposing forces, 'uplift from below and destruction from above', so 'contest' means a struggle between them. 'Game' and 'debate' are kinds of contest between people and do not fit natural forces.

questions.s: According to the passage, the rock between the Indian and Eurasian plates was pushed upwards because
o: the Eurasian plate was moving south
the old ocean floor was very light
neither plate could easily sink below the other
glaciers had worn away the rock below
questions.e: The passage states that 'neither plate could sink easily beneath the other' because both carried light continental crust, so the rock 'crumpled, folded and was pushed upwards.' It is the Indian plate that the passage says moved, northwards; nothing is said about Eurasia moving south.

questions.s: The discovery of fossils of sea creatures high in the mountains most directly supports which idea in the passage?
o: The mountain rock once lay beneath an ocean.
Glaciers carried sea creatures up the slopes.
Erosion is wearing the peaks down quickly.
Earthquakes are common in northern Pakistan.
questions.e: The author presents the fossils as 'evidence of the ancient ocean': rock that formed under the sea was pushed up by the collision. Glaciers are mentioned only as agents of erosion that wear the peaks down, not as carriers of fossils, and the fossils say nothing about earthquakes or the speed of erosion.

questions.s: Which of the following best describes how the passage is organised?
o: It compares two cities and argues that one is better planned.
It tells the story of one family's experience of a heatwave.
It presents a theory and then gives evidence against it.
It names an effect, explains its causes and results, and notes remedies.
questions.e: The passage names the urban heat island effect, explains its causes (materials, waste heat, blocked breezes, loss of trees), describes its consequences (health, electricity demand) and ends with simple remedies. Lahore is the only city mentioned, so there is no comparison of two cities, and no theory is disputed.

questions.s: According to the passage, cities cool down less at night than the countryside mainly because
o: roads and buildings release stored heat slowly
trees release water vapour into the city air
cities receive more sunlight during the day
farmland sends its heat towards the city
questions.e: The passage says asphalt, concrete and dark roofs 'absorb sunlight during the day and release the stored heat slowly after sunset, so cities cool down far less at night'. Water vapour from trees cools the air, the opposite of the effect asked about.

questions.s: The passage suggests that painting roofs in light, reflective colours helps because such roofs
o: release water vapour that cools the air
block breezes from entering the buildings
absorb less sunlight and so store less heat
reduce the number of vehicles on the roads
questions.e: Earlier the passage blames 'dark rooftops' that 'absorb sunlight during the day and release the stored heat'. A light, reflective roof does the reverse, absorbing less sunlight and so storing less heat. Releasing water vapour is how trees cool the air, not roofs.

questions.s: According to the passage, the word 'algorithm' comes from
o: the Latin form of al-Khwarizmi's name
the name of the House of Wisdom
questions.e: The passage says that in the Latin translation 'his name was written as Algoritmi, the origin of the modern word algorithm.' Al-jabr is the source of 'algebra', not 'algorithm', which makes it the most tempting wrong choice.

questions.s: According to the end of the passage, al-Khwarizmi's main importance lay in
o: finding a clever trick for each problem
giving general methods for types of problems
questions.e: The end of the passage says he 'grouped problems into types and gave step-by-step procedures that worked for every case of a type', and that his importance lay in this approach. It explicitly contrasts this with 'solving each problem by a special trick'. The passage says he explained a symbol for zero, not that he discovered it.

questions.s: It can be inferred from the passage that al-Khwarizmi's ideas reached European readers mainly through
o: lectures he gave in European cities
Greek copies made in the House of Wisdom
questions.e: Both European words linked to him arrived 'through later Latin translations': algebra from the title of one book and algorithm from the Latin form of his name in another. The House of Wisdom translated works into Arabic, not into Greek, and the passage never mentions him travelling to Europe.

questions.s: In the passage, the phrase 'traced to' most nearly means
questions.e: Random division makes the groups alike, 'so that any difference in results can be traced to the drug', meaning the difference can be attributed to, or explained by, the drug. 'Copied from' and 'drawn around' are literal senses of trace that make no sense with results.

questions.s: According to the passage, volunteers are divided into groups at random so that
o: doctors can choose who receives the drug
the groups are alike except for their treatment
the placebo looks the same as the real drug
more volunteers receive the new medicine
questions.e: The passage says random division 'makes the groups similar in age, health and other factors', so the treatment is the only real difference. The placebo looks identical because of how it is made, not because of the random division.

questions.s: The author would most likely agree that a trial in which the doctors know which patients receive the drug
o: is more reliable, as doctors can watch the drug group closely
is acceptable as long as the patients themselves do not know
may give misleading results even if the doctors are honest
cannot include a placebo group of any kind at all
questions.e: The author warns that doctors who knew might, 'without meaning to', encourage some patients more or judge symptoms differently, so bias can arise without dishonesty. The second option is tempting, but the author calls trials in which neither patients nor doctors know 'the best', so hiding the facts from patients alone is not enough.

questions.s: The passage is mainly about
o: the dangers of driving on long highways
the history of goods transport in Pakistan
a decorative tradition and the skills behind it
the poetry written by Pakistani truck drivers
questions.e: The passage describes what truck art looks like, how it is made in workshops by skilled craftsmen and what it means to drivers, then notes its spread to other objects. Poetry is mentioned only as one feature painted on trucks, and nothing says the drivers wrote it.

questions.s: In the passage, the word 'ornament' in 'far more than ornament' most nearly means
questions.e: The sentence contrasts mere decoration with the deeper meaning the painting has for drivers: pride and 'a home away from home'. 'Ornament' therefore means decoration. Nothing in the passage suggests the paintwork advertises anything or protects the vehicle.

questions.s: Which statement about truck art is best supported by the passage?
o: It is now made mainly for exhibitions abroad.
Each truck is decorated by one skilled painter.
Its regional styles have become almost identical.
It has personal meaning for the drivers.
questions.e: The passage says a painted truck 'reflects the pride of its owner' and is 'a home away from home' for drivers. The passage says a truck passes through the hands of carpenters, metalworkers and painters, so one painter is wrong, and observers can still tell regional styles apart.

questions.s: The author compares the glaciers to 'a giant water tower' because they
o: are taller than any building on the plains
store winter snow and release it in summer
hold back lakes behind walls of loose rock
send drinking water to cities through pipes
questions.e: The comparison is explained in the same sentence: 'snow that falls in winter is stored as ice and released as meltwater in summer'. Like a water tower, the glaciers store water and release it when it is needed. Holding back lakes is done by heaps of rock and ice left by retreating glaciers, not by the glaciers acting as stores.

questions.s: According to the passage, the natural dams that hold back glacial lakes are weak because they
o: consist of loose rock and ice
are melted by warm lake water
questions.e: The lakes are 'held back by loose heaps of rock and ice that the glacier left behind', and the next sentence calls such dams weak. The dams are natural, so concrete plays no part.

questions.s: It can be inferred that mapping which lakes are growing fastest is useful mainly because
o: it shows which glaciers have stopped melting
it allows the lakes to be drained more quickly
equipment can then go where the risk is greatest
it proves that average temperatures are rising
questions.e: The final sentence says mapping 'helps decide where such equipment is most needed', implying sensors and alarms cannot be placed everywhere and should go to the lakes most likely to burst. The passage never mentions draining lakes, and growing lakes indicate melting, not glaciers that have stopped melting.

questions.s: According to the passage, the sour taste of yogurt comes from
o: sugar added along with the starter spoonful
proteins that unfold when milk is heated
microbes that spoil milk left overnight
acid that bacteria make from milk sugar
questions.e: Lactic acid bacteria 'feed on lactose, the natural sugar in milk, and convert it into lactic acid', and the passage adds that this is 'why it tastes sour'. The proteins unfold because of the acid, not because of heating, and they explain the thickness rather than the taste.

questions.s: The author mentions the household advice about testing milk with a fingertip in order to
o: show that a common practice has a scientific reason
warn readers against touching milk that is boiling
suggest that thermometers give unreliable readings
explain why yogurt keeps longer than fresh milk
questions.e: The advice follows the explanation that bacteria die in milk that is too hot and multiply too slowly in milk that is too cold; 'This explains the common household advice' links the practice to that science. Thermometers are never mentioned, and keeping quality is explained separately by the acid.

questions.s: Based on the passage, what would most likely happen if the starter were stirred into milk that was still very hot?
o: The yogurt would set faster and taste more sour.
The milk would set but taste sweeter than usual.
The milk would fail to set into yogurt.
The proteins would link together at once.
questions.e: The passage states that if the milk is too hot when the starter is added, 'the bacteria die'. With no living bacteria, no lactic acid is made, so the proteins never link up and the milk does not set. The first option reverses this: heat kills the bacteria rather than speeding them up.

questions.s: According to the passage, why does a rise in the price of flour count for more than a rise in the price of ice cream?
o: Flour is sold in far more shops than ice cream.
Flour takes a larger share of household budgets.
Ice cream prices are not tracked by the index.
Ice cream prices rise more slowly than flour.
questions.e: Each item 'is weighted according to how much of a household budget it usually takes', and a typical family spends far more on flour than on ice cream. Ice cream is still in the index; its price simply carries less weight.

questions.s: As used in the passage, the phrase 'keep pace' most nearly means
questions.e: Wages and savings that 'fail to keep pace' with rapid inflation do not rise as quickly as prices, as the next sentence's example of a five per cent income rise against twelve per cent price rise shows. 'Remain unchanged' is wrong because the family's income does rise, just not fast enough.

questions.s: According to the reasoning of the passage, a worker whose monthly wage rises from 20,000 to 22,000 rupees in a year when prices rise by fifteen per cent
o: has a higher real income than before
has a lower real income than before
has the same real income as before
cannot be judged without her savings
questions.e: The wage rises by 2,000 out of 20,000, which is ten per cent, while prices rise by fifteen per cent, so the wage buys less than before. This is the passage's five-against-twelve example in new numbers. 'Higher' is the trap: she earns more rupees, but her real income has fallen.

questions.s: The main purpose of the passage is to
o: describe how dreams are recorded in sleep laboratories
argue that students should study only at night
compare the sizes of the hippocampus and the cortex
explain evidence that sleep helps us learn
questions.e: The passage moves from the old view of sleep as a pause to experiments and brain recordings showing that 'sleep plays an active part in learning', then draws a lesson for students. It actually warns against studying through the night, so the second option reverses its message.

questions.s: In the passage, the word 'regarded' in the first sentence most nearly means
questions.e: Sleep 'was regarded as little more than a pause' means it was considered or thought of as a pause. 'Respected' is another sense of regard, but it clashes with 'little more than', which shows a low opinion of sleep.

questions.s: Why does the experiment described in the passage compare volunteers who learned in the evening with those who learned in the morning?
o: to test whether people learn more easily in the evening
to keep the delay equal, so sleep is the main difference
to measure how long the hippocampus stores word pairs
to show that tired people cannot learn word pairs at all
questions.e: Both groups are tested twelve hours after learning, and the passage stresses that 'the same amount of time has passed'; only the evening group sleeps in between. Equal delays leave sleep as the key difference. The study compares memory after sleep, not ease of learning at different times, so the first option misreads its design.

questions.s: According to the passage, the membrane used in reverse osmosis
o: lets water pass but stops dissolved salts
boils the seawater while using very little fuel
turns the leftover brine back into drinking water
never needs to be cleaned or replaced at all
questions.e: The membrane's pores are 'so small that water molecules can pass through but dissolved salts cannot.' Boiling belongs to the older method, and the passage says the membranes 'must be cleaned or replaced regularly'.

questions.s: As used in the passage, the word 'attractive' in 'an attractive option' most nearly means
questions.e: Desalination is attractive to coastal cities 'because the sea will never run dry', so the word means appealing or worth considering. 'Good-looking' is the everyday sense for people and objects, but a supply option is not being judged on its looks.

questions.s: According to the passage, which of the following would most directly reduce the cost of desalinated water?
o: building the plant farther from the coast
releasing all the brine at a single outlet
making the pores of the membrane smaller
cheaper electricity to run the pumps
questions.e: The passage says desalinated water costs more 'mainly because of the electricity used', so cheaper electricity would cut the cost most directly. Releasing brine at one outlet is what the passage warns against, since it harms sea life near the outlet.

questions.s: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?
o: Fast rail travel made shared standard times necessary.
Noon arrives earlier in eastern towns than in western ones.
Single-track railways were the most dangerous form of travel.
The Royal Observatory at Greenwich was built for the railways.
questions.e: The passage shows how local sun time worked until railways arrived, why train timetables needed a common time, and how standard time and then time zones followed. The fact about noon in eastern towns is true in the passage but is only background to that main idea.

questions.s: According to the passage, why could local times be dangerous on single-track lines?
o: Station clocks often stopped working when trains passed.
Drivers were unable to see the sun at noon in tunnels.
Two trains might be sent towards each other on one line.
Horses near the track were frightened by passing trains.
questions.e: The passage explains that with each stop on its own time, 'two trains might be sent towards each other in the belief that the line was clear.' Horses are mentioned only as the older, slower form of travel, not as a danger on the railway.

questions.s: It can be inferred that, before the railways, the small differences between towns' times 'hardly mattered' because
o: every town already set its clocks by Greenwich
journeys were too slow for small gaps to matter
noon came at the same moment in every town
riders carried their own very accurate clocks
questions.e: The passage contrasts horse travel with trains that 'could cross a country in hours'. On slow journeys a difference of a few minutes between towns had no practical effect. Noon did not come at the same moment everywhere; the passage says it arrives earlier in eastern places.

questions.s: According to the passage, the openings in the street drains allowed
o: rainwater to flow into the wells
people to bathe in the street
salt to escape from the soil
questions.e: The drains 'had openings at intervals so that they could be cleaned.' Wells and bathing areas are described as features of the houses, not of the drains.

questions.s: According to the passage, why does much of our knowledge of Mohenjo-daro come from buildings and objects rather than written records?
o: Its people had no system of writing.
Its records were destroyed by salt.
Its seals were lost after excavation.
Its script has not yet been read.
questions.e: The passage says the people 'used a script found on thousands of small seals, but no one has yet been able to read it, so' knowledge comes from buildings and objects. The first option is the trap: they did write, but their writing cannot be understood. Salt is said to damage the bricks, not records.

questions.s: The author's attitude towards the planning of Mohenjo-daro can best be described as
questions.e: The author says what 'most impresses visitors' is 'the careful planning of ordinary life' and goes on to describe the grid streets, standard bricks and covered drains with evident approval. Nothing in the passage questions or criticises the planning, so 'doubtful' and 'disapproving' do not fit.

questions.s: In the passage, the phrase 'keep it in check' most nearly means
questions.e: Insects and diseases in the Amazon limit the plant's growth; without them elsewhere it spreads unchecked. To 'keep it in check' therefore means to keep it under control. 'Examine it closely' uses the other sense of check, as in checking work.

questions.s: According to the passage, a thick mat of water hyacinth harms fish mainly because
o: fish become trapped among its long roots
its flowers are poisonous to fish
weevils on it feed on fish eggs
rotting plants below it use up oxygen
questions.e: The mat 'blocks sunlight from the water below, so underwater plants die, and their decay uses up oxygen that fish need.' The weevils in the passage feed only on water hyacinth, so the third option misreads them.

questions.s: According to the passage, water hyacinth first spread around the world because people
o: grew it in gardens for its beauty
used it as feed for their cattle
planted it to clean polluted rivers
mistook it for a useful crop
questions.e: The passage says people 'carried it to gardens and ponds around the world for its beauty.' Its use as animal feed is described only at the end, as a way of using plants that have already been harvested as a weed.

questions.s: The author mentions that looking at the sun hurts the eyes in order to
o: show that the camera obscura can damage vision
explain why the image on the wall is upside down
support the idea that light enters the eye
warn readers against repeating his experiments today
questions.e: The example follows his claim that 'light travels in straight lines from objects into the eye', and the passage says the pain 'is hard to explain if the eye only sends rays out.' It is evidence for light entering the eye; the camera obscura is a separate example that comes afterwards.

questions.s: If a famous earlier scholar's claim disagreed with his experiments, Ibn al-Haytham, as described in the passage, would most likely have
o: accepted the claim because of the scholar's fame
trusted the results of his repeated experiments
altered his measurements to match the claim
questions.e: The passage says he insisted that claims be checked against controlled, repeated experiments and that 'even respected authorities' be examined critically. He would therefore trust careful evidence over reputation. Accepting the claim because of fame is exactly what his method rejects.

questions.s: As used in the passage, the word 'pioneer' most nearly means
questions.e: Historians call him 'an early pioneer of the experimental approach', meaning one of the first to develop it, a forerunner. 'Settler' is the literal sense of pioneer, someone who opens up new land, which does not fit a scholar's method.

questions.s: According to the passage, fixed solar panels in Pakistan are usually tilted towards the south because
o: dust collects less on south-facing panels
the wind usually blows from the south
the country lies north of the equator
southern roofs stay cooler in summer
questions.e: The passage says panels work best facing the sun directly, 'so in Pakistan, which lies north of the equator, fixed panels are usually tilted towards the south.' Dust is discussed as a separate problem, and nothing links it to the direction a panel faces.

questions.s: In the passage, the word 'enemy' in 'Dust is another enemy' most nearly means
questions.e: The next sentence explains that dust 'blocks part of the light' and reduces output, so 'enemy' is used figuratively for something that does harm. Dust cannot be a personal opponent or rival, which are senses that apply only to people.

questions.s: Which of the following can most reasonably be inferred from the passage?
o: Panels in Multan always produce less electricity than those in cooler cities.
Panels with moving parts usually last longer than those without them.
Cleaning panels makes little difference to their output in dry regions.
Of two panels in equal sunlight, the hotter one may give less power.
questions.e: The passage states that cells 'become less efficient as they get hotter', so with the same light the hotter panel can produce less. The first option is too strong: the passage compares one panel on a hot June afternoon with a cool spring day and says it 'may' produce less, not that Multan's panels always do.

questions.s: The passage is mainly concerned with
o: how plastic bags and bottles are manufactured
the nature, spread and effects of microplastics
why synthetic clothes ought to be banned worldwide
how sea ice forms in the Arctic each winter
questions.e: The passage defines microplastics, traces where they travel and what they may do to living things, and ends with how best to respond. Synthetic clothes appear only as one source of fibres; the passage never argues for a ban.

questions.s: According to the passage, microplastics are plastic fragments that
o: float on the surface of the sea
come only from face scrubs and clothes
are less than five millimetres across
have been swallowed by sea creatures
questions.e: The passage gives the definition directly: 'Fragments less than five millimetres across are called microplastics.' Face scrubs and clothes are only some of the sources; most come from larger items breaking down, so 'only' makes the second option wrong.

questions.s: The author's attitude towards the effects of microplastics on human health is best described as
questions.e: The author reports that researchers 'stress' that the effects on human health 'are not yet well understood', neither raising alarm nor brushing the issue aside. 'Alarmed' is tempting because the passage describes harm to animals, but it makes no claim of harm to people.

questions.s: As used in the passage, the word 'awkward' in 'slow and awkward' most nearly means
questions.e: Barter is awkward because the farmer must find a trader with exactly the right wants or arrange a chain of trades, so the word means inconvenient or difficult to manage. 'Shy' and 'embarrassing' describe awkward feelings in people, which do not fit a system of exchange.

questions.s: A family keeps some money in a drawer to pay school fees next year. According to the passage, this is an example of money acting as
questions.e: The passage calls money a store of value because it 'can be saved for later use', unlike wheat, which may spoil. It becomes a medium of exchange only when it is actually spent on the fees next year.

questions.s: The closing sentences suggest that money works mainly because
o: it is always made of a valuable metal
banks keep a record of every coin in use
people trust others to accept it later
questions.e: The passage ends: money 'works because people trust that it will be accepted tomorrow', which echoes the earlier point that people accept money because 'others will accept it in turn'. Most money today exists only as numbers in bank records, so valuable metal cannot be the reason.

questions.s: The question in the middle of the passage mainly serves to
o: introduce the weather's role in winter smog
suggest that pollution sources disappear in summer
criticise the factories and kilns of the Punjab
move the discussion from smog to lung disease
questions.e: The question is followed at once by 'Part of the answer lies in the weather' and the explanation of temperature inversions. The question itself states that the sources 'produce pollution all year round', so the second option contradicts it.

questions.s: According to the passage, during a temperature inversion the air near the ground is
o: warmer than the air above it
colder than the air above it
questions.e: On calm winter nights 'the air touching it becomes colder than the layer above. This situation is called a temperature inversion.' Warmer air near the ground is the normal situation that the inversion reverses, which makes it the tempting wrong choice.

questions.s: In the passage, the warm layer is said to act 'like a lid' because it
o: heats the ground during the cold night
blows the smog towards the cities
cleans pollutants out of the air
traps the polluted air beneath it
questions.e: The passage explains the comparison straight away: 'the cold, polluted air beneath cannot rise', so pollution builds up as if under a lid. The passage says the ground cools quickly at night, so the warm layer does not heat it.

questions.s: Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?
o: Well-organised volunteers can add much to scientific research.
Amateur astronomers have found more comets than professionals.
Data from untrained observers can never be trusted.
Mobile phones have replaced laboratories in modern science.
questions.e: The passage explains what volunteers contribute, why their numbers and spread matter, and how careful project design makes their data reliable. The worry that untrained observers are unreliable is presented as an old criticism that designers have answered, not as the author's view.

questions.s: Based on the passage, volunteer records would probably be least reliable for
o: common garden birds seen every day
the amount of rain falling at a school
a rare insect resembling several others
a familiar butterfly in its usual region
questions.e: Studies found volunteer and expert data broadly similar for 'common, easily recognised species, though less so for rare or confusing ones.' A rare insect that looks like several others is both rare and confusing. Common birds and a familiar butterfly fall into the reliable group.

questions.s: According to the passage, computer programs are used in citizen science projects to
o: point out records that look unusual
replace the work of professional experts
train new volunteers to count species
questions.e: Designers 'use computer programs to flag records that look unusual, such as a tropical bird reported in a snowy region.' Photographs are checked by experts, not identified automatically by programs, so the first option misreads the passage.

questions.s: According to the passage, waste buried in a landfill releases methane because it
o: is mixed with too many brown materials
is turned too often by workers
is too dry for microbes to act
questions.e: The passage says landfill waste is cut off from air and broken down by microbes that do not need oxygen, and ‘That process releases methane’. Brown materials are part of good composting, not the cause of landfill methane.

questions.s: According to the passage, a compost heap that smells bad should be
o: given more fresh grass and peels
covered tightly to keep out air
questions.e: A bad smell means the heap is too wet or has too much green material, and ‘adding browns and turning it solves the problem’. Fresh grass and peels are green materials, so adding them would make the smell worse.

questions.s: Which of the following can be inferred from the passage?
o: Composting food scraps can cut the methane that landfills release.
Compost heaps generally give off more methane than landfill sites.
Microbes in compost heaps work best when they are cut off from air.
Torn cardboard should never be added to a compost heap at all.
questions.e: Landfill methane comes from waste broken down without oxygen, while composting uses microbes that need oxygen and is called ‘a better route’; so diverting scraps to compost reduces that methane. The passage says heaps should be turned to let in air, which rules out the third option.

questions.s: According to the passage, bees turn nectar into honey mainly by
o: mixing it with water from the hive
storing it in sealed clay pots
questions.e: The passage says bees fan the nectar with their wings ‘until most of the water evaporates’, leaving a thick syrup. Hydrogen peroxide is produced slowly by the enzyme later; the bees do not add it directly.

questions.s: The passage suggests that dipping a wet spoon into a jar of honey is unwise because it
o: adds water that lets yeasts begin to ferment it
causes the honey to crystallise into hard, solid grains
removes the enzyme added by the bees
turns the honey too acidic to eat
questions.e: Honey's defences work only while it stays thick, and a wet spoon is given as an example of how it can absorb water so that ‘yeasts can begin to ferment it’. Crystallising is described as harmless and is caused by sugar leaving solution, not by a wet spoon.

questions.s: As used in the passage, the word ‘defences’ refers to
o: the walls and wax of the beehive
the stings carried by worker bees
the warnings printed on honey jars
questions.e: ‘These defences’ sums up the three features just described: high sugar that draws water from microbes, acidity and hydrogen peroxide. Stings are a bee's defence, but the passage never mentions them.

questions.s: According to the passage, the main cause of tides is
questions.e: The second sentence states that tides ‘are caused mainly by the Moon's gravity’. The Sun's effect is a little less than half the Moon's, and the shape of the coast only changes the size of the tides.

questions.s: According to the passage, spring tides occur when
o: the Sun and Moon pull at right angles
the Sun, Moon and Earth lie in a line
the Moon is farthest from the Earth
questions.e: The passage says that when the Sun, Moon and Earth lie in a line, at new and full moon, their effects combine to give spring tides. A right-angle pull at the quarter moons produces the weaker neap tides instead.

questions.s: The author's remark that spring tides ‘have nothing to do with the season’ is most likely included to
o: show that tides are unaffected by the Sun
correct a misunderstanding caused by the name
explain why neap tides occur at quarter moons
suggest that tides are strongest in spring
questions.e: The remark begins ‘Despite the name’, showing that the author expects readers to link spring tides with the spring season and wants to correct this; they occur about twice every month. The passage says the Sun does raise tides, so the first option is wrong.

questions.s: According to the passage, Popper believed a theory is scientific only if it
o: has been proved true by many observations
is accepted by most working scientists
could in principle be shown to be false
questions.e: The passage says a theory is scientific only if it is falsifiable, ‘so that an observation could in principle show it to be false’. The swan example shows why many agreeing observations cannot prove a theory true.

questions.s: The fortune-teller's prediction is mentioned as an example of a claim that
o: has been tested and shown to be false
cannot be proved wrong by any outcome
takes a clear and useful risk
questions.e: The passage says the prediction ‘can never be shown wrong, and that is exactly the weakness’ of it; it fits any outcome and so tells us nothing. It is the opposite of a theory that takes a risk.

questions.s: Which statement best describes how the author treats Popper's view?
o: The author rejects it as completely mistaken and outdated.
The author accepts every part of it without any reservation.
The author notes criticism but says its core still holds.
The author argues that it applies only to the study of birds.
questions.e: The author reports a criticism, that scientists do not drop a theory after one disagreeing result, but then writes ‘Even so, his central idea remains widely taught’. That is neither full rejection nor acceptance without reservation.

questions.s: According to the passage, the change in locust behaviour is triggered by
o: the colour of the plants they eat
questions.e: The passage says ‘Crowding sets off a remarkable transformation’: repeated touching of the hind legs causes chemical changes in the nervous system. Wind is mentioned only for how far a swarm travels once it has formed.

questions.s: As used in the passage, the word ‘solitary’ most nearly means
questions.e: The next sentence explains it: individual locusts ‘avoid one another’, so a solitary locust lives on its own. Nothing in the passage refers to the insects' sound or size.

questions.s: The last sentence of the passage makes the point that locust control is most successful when
o: it is carried out by one country alone
action is taken early, before swarms grow
swarms are attacked only after they have spread widely
farmers wait for the rains to stop
questions.e: The final sentence says stopping a swarm early, before it grows, is far cheaper and more effective than fighting it once it has spread. The passage also says control depends on cooperation between countries, so one country alone is wrong.

questions.s: According to the passage, the sarais built along the road were
o: tall brick pillars that marked distances
rows of trees planted for shade
roadside inns for travellers to rest
questions.e: The passage defines sarais as ‘roadside inns where travellers could rest and find water and food’. The brick pillars that marked distances were the kos minars, a separate feature.

questions.s: According to the passage, news travelled faster along the road because
o: the road was entirely resurfaced in the nineteenth century
trees gave shade to people walking along it
messengers could change to fresh horses at the sarais
traders carried letters between the towns
questions.e: The passage says messengers on horseback could change to fresh horses at the sarais, ‘so news travelled far faster than before’. The resurfacing came about three centuries later and is not linked to the speed of news.

questions.s: By calling the road ‘a river of life’, writers most likely mean that it
o: carried a constant, varied flow of people and culture
was often flooded by nearby rivers during the rainy season
followed the course of a major river
supplied water to the towns beside it
questions.e: The phrase comes right after the passage explains that people of many regions met and mixed along the road, spreading languages, foods, crafts and ideas; like a river, it carried a never-ending flow. Nothing in the passage mentions floods, so the image is not literal.

questions.s: According to the passage, the English word ‘checkmate’ comes from
o: the name chaturanga used in India
a Persian phrase about the king
a book of Arab chess puzzles
the name of a European queen
questions.e: The passage states that the Persian phrase shah mat, roughly ‘the king is helpless’, is the source of checkmate. Chaturanga is the name of the earliest Indian form of the game, not the origin of this word.

questions.s: According to the passage, games became faster at the end of the fifteenth century because
o: the game reached Spain and Italy
elephants and chariots were removed from the board
two pieces were given much greater range
questions.e: The adviser became the queen and could move any distance in any direction, and the elephant's successor could sweep whole diagonals, so ‘Attacks became faster’. The game had reached Spain and Italy about five centuries earlier, while games were still slow.

questions.s: The passage as a whole is mainly concerned with
o: the rules for winning a modern game of chess
how computers came to defeat world champions
how chess spread and changed over the centuries
why chess was first invented to train real armies in India
questions.e: The passage traces chess from India to Persia, the Arab world and Europe, then describes the rule change that made the modern game and its later use of computers. Deep Blue is one final example, and the army pieces only describe what chaturanga represented, not why it was invented.

questions.s: According to the passage, a bat judges how far away an object is from
o: the time an echo takes to return
the difference between its two ears
questions.e: The passage says the time an echo takes to return tells the bat how far away an object is. Differences between the sound at its two ears tell it the direction, not the distance.

questions.s: Spallanzani could not explain his results mainly because
o: the bats he tested were unable to fly in the dark
he could not hear the sounds the bats made
he had blocked the ears of every bat
questions.e: The passage says he could not explain how bats ‘see’ with their ears ‘since he heard nothing’; the calls were too high for human ears, which Griffin later showed with new equipment. The blinded bats did fly easily in the dark, so the first option contradicts the passage.

questions.s: The sentence ‘The insects have not been idle either’ suggests that
o: insects are generally more active than bats at night
moths have stopped flying near bats
bats no longer hunt moths at all
some prey have developed defences against bats
questions.e: The sentence introduces moths that hear bat calls and dive, and others that click to confuse the hunter: ways of fighting back against echolocation. ‘Not idle’ refers to these responses, not to how active insects are at night.

questions.s: According to the passage, the pink colour of much of Khewra's salt comes from
o: the coloured lights that are placed in the chambers
the brine pool inside the mine
small traces of minerals such as iron
the age of the ancient sea
questions.e: The passage says the pink or reddish colour ‘comes from small traces of other minerals, especially iron’, and that purer layers are white or clear. The illuminated chambers are a tourist feature and do not colour the salt itself.

questions.s: According to the passage, miners at Khewra leave about half the salt in place because
o: the remaining salt is too impure to sell
tourists visiting the mine want to see the original rock
the 1872 plan forbade any further digging
the pillars keep the roof from collapsing
questions.e: In the room-and-pillar method the salt is left as ‘thick columns that hold up the roof’, which is safer because salt creeps under heavy pressure. The passage admits this wastes salt, so it is not left because it is impure.

questions.s: As used in the passage, the word ‘creep’ most nearly means
questions.e: Salt that can ‘slowly creep and flow under heavy pressure’ changes shape little by little, which is why pillars are needed. Moving quietly to avoid notice is how a person creeps, a sense that does not fit rock.

questions.s: According to the passage, noise-cancelling headphones reduce steady noise mainly by
o: playing a reversed copy of the noise
sealing the ears completely with thick cushions
filtering the air around the ears
questions.e: Microphones pick up the noise and circuits produce ‘a matching wave that is exactly reversed’, which the speaker plays so that the waves cancel. The cushions matter mainly for sudden or high-pitched sounds, not for the steady noise the method targets.

questions.s: As used in the passage, the word ‘steady’ most nearly means
questions.e: Steady sounds such as an engine's hum are described as ones that ‘change slowly and are easy to predict’, so steady means constant. ‘Firmly fixed in one place’ is the sense used for a ladder or a table, not for a sound.

questions.s: Based on the passage, which of the following would noise-cancelling headphones most likely cancel least effectively?
o: the drone of an aircraft engine
the whirr of an air conditioner
the sudden bark of a dog
questions.e: The passage says sudden or high-pitched sounds change too quickly to be cancelled fully, while steady, low-pitched hums are cancelled best. A dog's sudden bark is the only sudden sound listed; the other three are steady hums like the engine and air conditioner in the passage.
